# Sūrah Al-Baqarah (Chapter 2) — Verse-by-Verse Tafsir

## Introduction to the Sūrah

This is the longest sūrah of the Book, and the first of the sūrahs revealed in Madinah in the order of the written text. It came down over a long stretch of the Prophet's life there, verse by verse and passage by passage, as the community in that city took shape and needed instruction, correction and law. The name it carries comes from a story told inside it, where Moses orders his people to slaughter a cow and they argue over which one was meant; the story became the sūrah's title because it captures so much of what the sūrah does. A people who had the truth in front of them kept asking for more detail until the simple command turned heavy, and the sūrah is full of that pattern. It opens with three letters, then divides all of humanity into those who believe, those who deny, and those who pretend, and it settles the foundation on which the rest of the Book stands.

The sūrah is not a single discourse but a set of them that belong to one purpose. It lays out who God is, what revelation is, and what the human being owes, and then it walks through the history of a community that was given the same trust before and lost its way. The story of the children of Israel runs through a great part of it, told as a warning and as a lesson for the new community, and the sūrah pauses to record the building of the House by Abraham and Ishmael, the prayer they made for a messenger to come from their descendants, and the answering of that prayer in the Prophet who recites these verses. From there the sūrah turns to law: fasting, prayer, alms, trade, debt, marriage, divorce, war and peace, so that the reader meets in one place both what to believe and how to live, and the two are held together as one subject rather than two.

Several of the Book's most particular treasures sit inside this sūrah. The greatest verse of the Book is here, the verse of the Throne, and so is the longest verse, which sets out the writing of a debt so that the rights of people are not lost. The change of direction in prayer is recorded here, and the fast of the month is commanded here, and the closing verses are a prayer of a community that God Himself taught to speak. The Prophet is remembered as saying that the two brightest sūrahs are al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, and a report carried by Muslim has Abū Hurayrah report that he warned the community not to turn their homes into graves, because the house in which al-Baqarah is recited is not entered by the deceiver. Another report, in the collection of al-Nasāʾī, has Ibn Masʿūd report that the deceiver leaves a house in which al-Baqarah is heard. Those reports place the sūrah in the middle of ordinary life, in a house and in a family, and not only in the study of a scholar.

The opening of the sūrah teaches the reader how to read it. Three letters come first, unexplained, so that the student learns from the very beginning that some of what God has sent down is his to measure and some of it is his to receive. Then the sūrah names the people it is writing for and the people it is warning, and it does not flatter either group. The believers are described by what they do and not by what they say; the deniers are told plainly that no argument will reach them; the pretenders are given the longest description of the three, because they are the hardest to see and the most dangerous to the community. What follows is a sūrah that a reader can spend a life inside, and the commentary on this chapter takes it verse by verse, beginning with the letters that stand at its head.

---

## Verse 2:1

> Alif-Lãm-Mĩm

**THE LETTERS THAT OPEN TWENTY-NINE SŪRAHS**

The sūrah begins with three letters: ***“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”***. They are read by their names and not by their sounds, so the reciter says alif, lām, mīm, and he does not join them into a word. Twenty-nine sūrahs of the Book open in this way, which means that a reader meets the device again and again and cannot dismiss it as an accident of one page. Some of these openings are single letters and some are longer combinations, and the letters are drawn from the ordinary alphabet of the Arabic tongue. The reader who has just finished asking God for guidance in the opening sūrah arrives here and is given a sentence he cannot work out for himself, and that is the first lesson of the chapter: the Book he is about to read contains matters that are settled by receiving them, not by solving them.

**WHAT HAS BEEN HANDED DOWN ABOUT THEM**

What the letters mean has been discussed since the earliest generations, and the answers that have come down differ. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with one reading in which the three letters stand for the three names that carry the message: alif for Allah, lām for the angel Gabriel who brought the revelation, and mīm for Muhammad who received it. He is also credited with other readings, one making the letters stand for God's blessings, kindness and dominion, and another making them the beginnings of three of God's names. The weight of the early community fell on leaving the meaning to God, and al-Shaʿbī and a group with him took that position: the letters are among the verses whose meaning is left to God, and the community believes them as they were sent down. That reading was held to be the secret of the Book, and a saying attributed to Abū Bakr puts it in a form worth remembering: every book has a secret, and the secret of this Book lies in the openings of its sūrahs.

**PARALLEL OPENINGS ACROSS THE BOOK**

The Book uses the same opening elsewhere, and the combinations there help the reader see the pattern without pretending to know more than he has been given. Another sūrah of the same kind begins with the identical three letters: (3:1 — **“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”**). A third adds a fourth letter to them: (7:1 — **“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd”**). The Book also announces, at the head of one of these sūrahs, that the revelation is from the Lord of all worlds and that no doubt belongs to it, which tells the reader what to expect after the letters are spoken. What the openings do is to catch the attention of a people who were proud of their language, and to remind them that the very sounds they use for poetry and trade stand at the door of a text they cannot match. The letters are common; the sentence built from them is not.

**A BOUNDARY DRAWN AROUND HUMAN KNOWLEDGE**

Think of a sealed envelope handed to a man who can read every word on the outside but cannot open it. He knows who sent it, because the seal says so, and he keeps it with the respect its sender deserves. The verse places the reader in that position on the first line of the chapter, and the position is not a humiliation but a discipline. These days a person can look up any fact within seconds and come to expect an answer for every question he meets, and the opening letters quietly deny him that expectation where God has chosen to withhold the answer. The reader is being taught that his knowledge has a boundary, and that the boundary is part of the message rather than a failure of it.

**UNMATCHED SPEECH BUILT FROM COMMON LETTERS**

The letters also stand at the head of a text that dares its readers to match it, and the sūrah makes the challenge a few lines later. The Book invites anyone who doubts the revelation to bring a single sūrah of its kind: (2:23 — **“then produce a sûrah like it”**), and it adds that the helpers they call on besides God will not make the difference. A reader who has followed the argument sees why the letters come first, because the challenge is made in the material the Arabs handled every day. They knew every letter; they had never produced a sentence like the one the letters introduce. The claim of the sūrah is not that the vocabulary is beyond them but that the arrangement is, and the argument holds today in a world that has more readers of Arabic than ever and still no rival to this text.

---

## Verse 2:2

> This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺

**A DECLARATION THAT POINTS AT SOMETHING ALREADY KNOWN**

The sūrah leaves the letters and speaks plainly: ***“This is the Book!”*** The sentence is a declaration, and the particle it opens with points at something honoured and known rather than at something near at hand. The generality of the earliest commentators read the two words as meaning that this is the Book, the one promised and expected, now standing in front of its readers. The distance in the wording carries its own point, because the demonstrative looks back over the whole of the opening sūrah and answers the request made there: the servant asked to be guided, and the answer is a Book that will do the guiding. The reader who finished al-Fātiḥah with a plea for the straight path meets the reply in the first clear sentence of al-Baqarah, and the arrangement is not a coincidence of editing but the shape of the revelation.

**THE CLAIM THAT NO DOUBT BELONGS TO IT**

The next phrase is a claim about the Book itself: ***“There is no doubt about it”***. Ibn ʿAbbās read it as meaning that the Book has come from God, and Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah and al-Suddī all read it in this way. It is recorded that no disagreement on the point was known among the early teachers. The wording does not say that everyone will be free of doubt; it says that no doubt belongs to the Book, and the difference matters. A doubt is something the doubter brings, and the sūrah goes on in the following verses to describe people who carry it and are not moved by any argument. The same claim is made in another sūrah about the revelation as a whole: (32:2 — **“The revelation of this Book is—beyond doubt—from the Lord of all worlds”**). What the reader is being handed at the start of the longest sūrah is therefore a firm surface, and the firmness is claimed before any of the contents have been shown.

**THE QUALIFICATION THAT THE BOOK SETS ON ITSELF**

The verse does not stop at certainty, and its last phrase names the people the Book will guide: ***“a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. The word carries the sense of guarding oneself from harm, and the sūrah describes its people in that language again at the end of a passage that lists what they do and what they give: (2:177 — **“it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”**). The guidance is stated as a fact about the Book, and the qualification is stated as a condition of receiving it. The early authorities put the point plainly, reading the phrase as meaning that the Book guides the one who comes to it with the intention of guarding himself from what God has forbidden. A reader who opens the Book to win an argument will find material for an argument; the one who opens it to be corrected will find the correction. The difference is not in the Book, which is the same for both, but in what they brought to it.

**TWO TRAVELLERS AND A WELL-MARKED ROAD**

Think of two men driving the same road at night. Both pass the same signs, and one arrives while the other takes a wrong turning and blames the signs. The signs did not change between them; the driver who arrived read them with the intention of obeying them. The verse says the Book is guidance and then says it is guidance for the mindful, and the two statements together tell the reader where the difference lies. These days a person can have the whole text on his phone and never once open it with the intention of being corrected, and the verse quietly denies him the excuse of the sign. What the passage asks of the reader is simple to state and hard to keep: come to the Book to be told what to do, and the guidance that is already in it will reach him. The verse also protects the reader from a common mistake, which is to measure the Book by the behaviour of the people who claim it and then walk away when the behaviour disappoints him, because the claim of this sentence is about the Book and not about its readers.

---

## Verse 2:3

> who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them

**BELIEF WORSHIP AND OPEN-HANDED TRUST**

The verses that follow describe the people the Book will guide, and the description begins with what they hold to be true: ***“who believe in the unseen, establish prayer”***. The unseen is what is hidden from the senses, and the early authorities named the things it covers: the resurrection, the reckoning, the scale, the bridge, Paradise and the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with that list and with a wider reading in which the unseen includes whatever God has kept from human sight, including God Himself, who is not seen in this life. The second mark in the phrase is the prayer, and the wording here is not the word for praying once but for standing the prayer up and keeping it standing. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the phrase as performing the prescribed prayers in full, with their ablution, their bowing, their prostration and their appointed times, which makes the mark a matter of practice rather than of feeling.

The order of the marks is worth noticing, because the sūrah puts belief first and worship second. A person can pray without believing what he is told about God, and the prayer then becomes a habit that carries him nowhere; a person can believe and never pray, and the belief sits in him untested and slowly cools. The verse puts belief first and worship second, in the order of root and fruit. The Book repeats the pair elsewhere in a single sentence about the same people, and the reason for noticing it is that the description here is the standard and not a local arrangement: (8:3 — **“those who establish prayer and donate from what We have provided for them”**). What the reader is given at the head of the sūrah is therefore a portrait with its features in order, and the order tells him where to begin when his own practice has slipped.

**THE THIRD MARK AND WHY IT COMES LAST**

The third mark closes the verse: ***“and donate from what We have provided for them”***. The wording does not say from what they own, and the difference is deliberate. What a person holds is a provision given to him, which makes the gift an act of handling someone else's property in the way the owner intended. The early authorities read the phrase widely, some taking it as the obligatory poor-due and others as every act of giving in obedience to God, and the second reading does not cancel the first. The Book joins giving to prayer again in the same wording used here for the same people: (2:45 — **“seek help through patience and prayer”**) sits in a passage that sends the reader to the two instruments of patience and worship, and the giving in this verse belongs to the same family of habits. A community that prays and never gives can hold its worship inside itself, and the sūrah closes the door on that possibility on its first page. The reasoning behind the order is that a closed hand and a closed heart usually travel together, since the gift is what proves that the giver has stopped treating his provision as his own.

**TRUST BEFORE SIGHT**

A reader may wonder why the verse begins with what cannot be seen when so much of the Book deals with what can. The answer lies in what belief does to a person: it forms him around something he cannot check, and from that formation the actions in the rest of the verse draw their weight. Ibn Masʿūd said that belief is trust, and al-Zuhrī is credited with describing it as the deeds themselves, which shows how closely the earliest teachers tied the inner thing to the outer. A man who obeys only what he can see is obeying the visible authority in the room; the man who obeys the unseen has accepted a Lord over the whole of his life, including the parts no observer will ever see. The three marks in the verse are therefore one movement: a heart that trusts what it cannot see, a body that stands in prayer at the appointed time, and a hand that opens from what it has been given. That is why the verse reads as a single portrait rather than as three separate requirements, and the point is that a person who has grown in one of them is being pulled towards the other two.

**A SERVER WHO KEEPS A LEDGER IN TWO COLUMNS**

Think of a servant who is entrusted with a shop and keeps two books, one for the owner and one for himself. He has learned to put everything into the first book, because the second is a fiction that the owner's arrival would expose in a single hour. The verse trains the reader in that habit. It asks him to hold what he cannot see as certain, to stand where he has been told to stand, and to spend as a man spending another's property. Anyone who has watched a person give up a good deal for a promise that had not yet arrived will recognise the shape of this verse, and anyone who has watched a person hold on to everything until his last day will recognise what the verse is saving him from. The instruction is plain today, in a time when the visible is louder than it has ever been.

---

## Verse 2:4

> and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter

**A FAITH THAT TAKES IN EVERY BOOK SENT DOWN**

The fourth mark of the mindful is stated in three parts, and the first concerns the revelation given to the Prophet: ***“and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺”***. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the phrase as belief in the Qur'an as the word of God, and with the further point that what is believed is not the paper and the ink but the message those carry. The address to the Prophet in the middle of a verse about his followers is worth noticing, because it keeps the messenger in view while the community is being described. A believer accepts what came to him through a man he never met, and he accepts it because of the One who sent it rather than because of any evidence he gathered first. The same faith is asked of the community in a verse addressed to believers as a command: (4:136 — **“the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before”**). The revelation is one act of God with more than one delivery, and the verse begins by naming the latest of them.

**THE EARLIER REVELATION AND THE ONE PEOPLE WHO RECEIVED IT**

The second part widens the same belief to everything sent before: ***“and what was revealed before you”***. The early authorities read this as the Scriptures given to the prophets of earlier communities, and the Book itself names what was given to Moses and to Jesus and to the prophets who came between them. Ibn ʿAbbās understood this as the believer’s affirmation that all of it came from the same Lord, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah and others described the believers here as those who accept every book that God sent down. The wording does not ask the reader to follow the earlier Scriptures in their present form, a point the sūrah returns to later when it speaks about their preservation and their readers. What it does ask is that he refuse to divide the messengers, and the Book states that refusal in the words of the believers themselves: (3:84 — **“we make no distinction between any of them”**). A community that thinks of itself as the first people God ever addressed will not carry the humility the verse is teaching, because the point of the phrase is that the road it walks was marked before it arrived. The difference between a newcomer and an heir shows itself in how each one treats the people who came earlier, and the verse is asking the reader to behave like an heir.

**THE CERTAINTY ABOUT THE LIFE TO COME**

The third part closes the verse: ***“and have sure faith in the Hereafter”***. The wording here is not the same as the word for belief used earlier in the same sentence; it carries assurance and settled conviction, as though the matter had been checked and put beyond dispute. Al-Suddī and Qatādah are credited with explaining it as certainty without doubt, and Ibn ʿAbbās with the reading that the Hereafter is certain in the heart of such a person and not merely repeated by his tongue. The Book uses the same phrase for the same people at the head of other sūrahs, where the description of the guided is repeated in almost the same order: (27:3 — **“have sure faith in the Hereafter”**). Placing it last among the marks is fitting, because a person's certainty about the return is what makes his prayer steady and his giving cheerful. Without that certainty the two are carried out as duties that may or may not matter in the end, and the reason the sūrah ends the description with it is that everything before it depends on it.

**A FAMILY THAT KEEPS LETTERS FROM SEVERAL SENDERS**

Think of a household that receives letters from a father who has written at different times and through different carriers. The family does not treat the earlier letters as belonging to someone else, and it does not obey the letter that suits them while shelving the rest. The verse forms the reader into a person who accepts the whole correspondence, the newest included, and who lives with his eyes on the appointment his father promised. These days it is easy to meet a person who is devoted to the newest thing and dismissive of everything old, and just as easy to meet the opposite, and the verse refuses both habits in a single line. It asks the reader to hold the revelation as one thing, delivered at different times, and to be as certain of the meeting it announces as he is of the day he can already count in his calendar.

---

## Verse 2:5

> It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful

**THE VERDICT PRONOUNCED ON THE PEOPLE JUST DESCRIBED**

After five verses of description the sūrah gives its verdict, and the verdict is a declaration from God about the people it has just named: ***“It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord”***. The wording is emphatic in both directions, since the pronoun singles them out and the guidance is traced to its source. What the earlier verses listed was the practice of the mindful, and this verse names what that practice produces: a guidance that comes down from their Lord and not from their own cleverness. For Ibn ʿAbbās, this guidance was a light in the heart by which a person sees the road, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas with the reading that it is the direction the Book gives to those who accept it. The two readings agree that guidance is a gift, and the sentence locates the giver: it is their Lord, the same Lord whose mercy was named at the head of the opening sūrah.

**THE VERDICT REPEATED IN ANOTHER SŪRAH**

The Book states the same verdict about the same kind of people in more than one place, which tells the reader that this is a settled description rather than a mood of one passage. Another sūrah uses almost these words when it finishes describing those who pray and give and are certain of the Hereafter: (31:5 — **“It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful”**). The repetition is not idle, because the reader who meets the sentence twice learns that the marks he is asked for are the marks of a type and not the qualifications of a list. A third sūrah opens with the result alone, before any of the marks have been named, so that the reader hears the verdict and then learns what earned it: (23:1 — **“Successful indeed are the believers”**). The sūrah al-Baqarah puts the description before the verdict, and the order lets the reader test himself against the parts before he hears the whole. What turns on the order is the reader's honesty, since a man who hears the verdict first may assume it covers him, while a man who reads the marks first has to ask whether they describe him.

**SUCCESS NAMED AFTER GUIDANCE**

The verse continues with a second promise: ***“and it is they who will be successful”***. The word carries more than a good outcome; it names the winning of what a person most needs, in a transaction where nothing can be added afterwards. The Book promises a share of God's mercy to those who obey, and it uses the language of success at the head of al-Baqarah to answer a fear that has run through the sūrah's opening verse, where the reader was told that a Book had come and that some would not be reached by it. Here the reader is told the opposite outcome in the same breath. Anyone who has worked for years at something and been told at the end that the effort stood for nothing will understand the weight of the promise, and anyone who has been told that the effort was accepted will understand why the verse ends on that word rather than on a description of the reward. The reason the wording carries no details of the reward is that the verdict itself is the comfort, and a servant who trusts his Lord does not need the account settled in advance.

**A FARMER WHO HEARS THE VERDICT BEFORE THE MARKET**

Think of a farmer who takes his crop to a market known for exact scales and honest buyers. He does not know the price when he arrives, but he knows the character of the men who will weigh what he brought. The verse names the scale and the outcome and leaves the details to the day itself. It also tells the reader where to look for reassurance, which is not in his own record but in the Lord who gave the guidance. These days success is measured by what can be counted and displayed, and the sūrah uses the same word for a result that nobody can show yet. The reader who finishes this verse is meant to walk out of it with a settled hope, and the hope rests on the One who spoke the verdict rather than on the strength of the one who heard it. The next verses describe the people who will not arrive, and the difference between the two groups is not the size of their effort but the direction of their trust.

---

## Verse 2:6

> As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe

**HEARTS SET AGAINST THE WARNING**

A sharp contrast now places the guided beside the people who will not arrive: ***“As for those who persist in disbelief”***. The sentence is placed immediately after the promise given to the mindful, and the placing is deliberate, because the two portraits sit side by side so that the reader can tell them apart. The Arabic word for disbelief carries the sense of covering something over, and al-Kalbī and others explained the group here as those who had heard the message and buried it. Ibn ʿAbbās named the leaders of Mecca and the men of the clans who had made themselves the enemies of the Prophet, and other early teachers named the Jews of Madinah, since both groups stood in the way of the message with full knowledge of it. The verse does not describe a person who never heard; it describes a person who heard, understood and covered the matter up.

**A WARNING REFUSED BEFORE IT ARRIVES**

The sentence continues with the statement that is meant to stop the Prophet from carrying a burden that is not his: ***“it is the same whether you warn them or not”***. The Arabic word for warning carries the sense of giving a person information that also frightens him, and the verse says the effort has been spent on the wrong kind of listener. Another sūrah states the same thing in almost the same words, and its repetition marks the sentence as a settled fact of the message: (36:10 — **“It is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe”**). The reason the sentence stands here is that the one who carried the message would grieve over people who would not answer him, and the sūrah removes the guilt before it can take root. A messenger is answerable for delivering the message, and the verse settles the difference between the delivery and the result. That the warning was sent at all is the proof that the caller did his work, and the answer belongs to the One who gave the warning its moment and its hearer.

**THE INVITATION THAT STILL STANDS**

A reader may take the verse as a reason to stop inviting people, and the reading is a mistake for a reason that the sūrah itself supplies. The verse is a statement about people whose case God has already judged, and it is addressed to the Prophet as comfort, not to the community as an instruction to give up. The Book commands the invitation in every period and describes no one as beyond it, and the door remains open until a person dies; the very next verses in this sūrah describe people who still have something to answer for. What turns on the difference is the state of the heart rather than the label a person carries, since the one who covers the truth today may be exposed to it tomorrow, and the Book tells the reader to keep speaking to him on that chance. The duty to invite is not suspended by the knowledge that God has recorded what a man will do, because the record is God's and the speech is the servant's. History is full of people who fought the message and then carried it, and the beginning of that road is a warning that reached them after all.

**A FIRE BRIGADE AND A HOUSE WITH NO EXITS**

Think of men who arrive at a burning house and find that the owner has nailed shut the doors from the inside. They shout through the boards, and the shouting is still the right thing to do, though it cannot reach a man who has decided to hear nothing. The verse tells the caller where his responsibility ends, and it does so without giving him permission to despise anyone. These days a person may find that his own family has stopped listening to the things he cares about most, and the passage spares him a false guilt while keeping his duty to speak with kindness. What follows in the sūrah explains why the doors were closed in the first place, and the explanation begins with the next verse, which names what happened to the instruments a person hears and sees with. The verse that carries the sentence of no belief ends the passage on a note that the reader should not soften: ***“they will never believe”*** while the covering lasts, and the reader is left with the difference between a warning that fails and a warning that was never given.

---

## Verse 2:7

> Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment

**THE CLOSING OF THE INSTRUMENTS THAT CARRY TRUTH**

The condition just described now receives its cause: ***“Allah has sealed their hearts”***. The word for sealing describes a stamp pressed onto something so that nothing further enters it, and the first generations understood it in that sense. Al-Suddī said that the sealing means God has stamped the hearts, and Mujāhid described the stamp as what settles on a heart once sin has made its home there and covered it. Qatādah gave the reading that the hearts were sealed when their owners obeyed the deceiver and kept disobeying, so that the seal was the outcome of a road they chose rather than a sentence passed on people who had never walked it. The verse is therefore not a description of an arbitrary act; it is the end of a process, and the sūrah has just described the group as those who persist.

**PUNISHMENT BEYOND THE SEALED FACULTIES**

The verse widens the closing to the other instruments a person is given: ***“and their hearing, and their sight is covered”***. The wording distinguishes between the two: the hearing is sealed with the heart, while the sight is described as having a covering laid over it, a veil that prevents the truth from arriving. The Book states the same condition again in a verse that lists the three together and traces the act to God: (16:108 — **“whose hearts, ears, and eyes are sealed by Allah”**). Another sūrah ends a passage about people who broke their pledges with nearly the same sentence: (7:101 — **“This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers”**). The point the reader is meant to carry away is that the instruments are not damaged on their own; they are the equipment by which a person lives, and the loss of them is the heaviest loss a person can suffer while still walking around. One teacher compared the condition to a lamp whose glass has been covered while the wick still burns, since the light is there and none of it reaches the road.

**THE OUTCOME THAT FOLLOWS THE CLOSING**

The verse finishes with the consequence: ***“They will suffer a tremendous punishment”***. The punishment is named in the future tense, and it is placed after the closing of the instruments so that the reader sees the order of events rather than a single verdict. Several early teachers drew a distinction here between two kinds of punishment, one that arrives in this life by the withdrawal of the help that would have led a person back, and the one kept for the Hereafter. The Book states the same withdrawal in a passage about those who were told the truth and turned away: (9:87 — **“their hearts have been sealed so they do not comprehend”**). What follows in this sūrah is a description of people who live among the believers, speak their language and intend them harm, and the verses about them make the most sense after the sealed hearts have been described, because the pretender is a person whose outward speech still works while the inward instruments have stopped. The passage therefore moves from the open enemy to the hidden one in a single step, and the hidden case is therefore far harder to detect.

**A CLOCK WHOSE SPRING HAS BEEN REMOVED**

Think of a clock that still hangs on the wall and still shows a face, but whose spring has been taken out. It is not broken in any way an observer can see, and it keeps the room looking furnished, yet it will never tell the time again. The verse describes people in that condition with respect to the truth, and the description is a warning to the reader rather than a curiosity about someone else. The warning lands hardest when a person notices how small the first steps are, because the road to a sealed heart starts with a preference defended once and then defended again. These days, when a person can arrange his attention so that nothing arrives that he did not choose, the verse reads as a description of a habit rather than of a distant punishment. What the reader is asked to do is to keep the instruments open and to act on what they carry while the capacity to act is still his.

---

## Verse 2:8

> And there are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers

**A NEW GROUP ENTERS THE SŪRAH**

The sūrah has described the guided and then the people who cover the truth, and now it names a third kind: ***“And there are some”***. The early teachers identified them as the pretenders, the people who lived inside the community and worked against it, and Ibn ʿAbbās read the opening as a description of people whose outward confession and inward state do not match. The Book gives this group more space at the head of the sūrah than it gives the deniers, and the reason is practical. A denier can be seen and counted; a pretender sits in the same gathering, speaks the same words and shares the same meals, and the harm he can do is larger because nobody knows where to stand in relation to him. The sūrah prepares the reader for that difficulty by naming the group before it describes their behaviour.

**PUBLIC CLAIM WITHOUT INNER FAITH**

The verse quotes what they say: ***“who say”***, ***“We believe in Allah”***, ***“and the Last Day”***. The claim is stated exactly, and the wording matters. The pretenders confessed faith in God and in the Day of Judgment and left the messenger out of the sentence, and the reason for the omission is easy to see, since naming him would have forced them into either a lie they could not manage or a denial that would have exposed them. The omission is a small thing in the mouth and a large thing in meaning, because the message of this Book is not a set of beliefs about God that a person can hold while standing apart from the man who brought it. The Book records their speech again in another sūrah and marks it with a witness of its own: (63:1 — **“but Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars”**). The reader is being shown a person who says the right words and is measured by something other than his words.

**CLAIM SPOKEN BACK TO ITS SPEAKERS**

The verse closes by denying the claim: ***“yet they are not ˹true˺ believers”***. The denial is placed after the quotation so that the reader hears the profession first and then hears the answer to it, and the two sit in one sentence without any argument between them. Ibn ʿAbbās read the closing as meaning that they do not believe secretly, whatever they announce openly, and al-Kalbī and others read the group as those whose inside and outside differ. The Book returns to the same people later and gives the reason their speech cannot carry them anywhere, since a confession made for an audience is measured by the audience and not by God: (4:142 — **“Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them”**). What turns on this verse for the reader is that speech is not the measure of faith in the Book, since the Book measures a person by a confession that his conduct confirms, and the next verses describe the conduct of these men in detail.

**TWO-FACED SPEECH UNDER ONE ROOF**

Think of a man who signs a contract to satisfy the people in the room while intending from the first day to break every clause that costs him anything. The signature is real and the paper is real, and none of it changes his position for a moment. The verse describes a party of such people inside the community, and it does so without any bitterness, because the reader is being taught to know what he is dealing with. These days the same type can be found in any institution, speaking the language of the group while working for something else, and the sūrah will describe them fully before it moves on to the people whose confession matches their conduct. What the reader is meant to take from the passage is caution about himself first, since the difference between the two groups is invisible from the outside and only the person himself knows which one he is. The passage is not an invitation to hunt for pretenders in a community, and the Book never asks the believers to appoint themselves as judges of what is hidden.

---

## Verse 2:9

> They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it

**THE ATTEMPT TO OUTWIT THE ONE WHO SEES**

The next verse explains what the pretenders are trying to do: ***“They seek to deceive Allah”***. The wording describes an attempt to cheat someone by showing him what he wants to see, and the early teachers took it in that sense. Ibn ʿAbbās read it as contravening God in secret while appearing to obey in public, and he added another reading in which the men were so bold that they imagined God Himself could be misled. The second reading sounds strange, and the reason the Book uses this language is that what these men actually did was try to deceive the messenger and the believers, so the attempt is traced to its true target, since an insult offered to the one who carries a message belongs to the sender of it. That is the point the verse is making, because the honour of a messenger belongs to the sender, and an insult offered to the one he sent is measured at its source.

**THE COMMUNITY THEY HOPED TO FOOL**

The verse names the community as well as God: ***“and the believers”***. The claim they were managing is not only a claim about God, who is hidden from them, but a claim about a group of people they could see every day, and the phrase shows how the pretenders understood their situation. Ibn ʿAbbās named Abū Bakr and the Companions as those they hoped to fool, and the Book records elsewhere the way the same men worked: (58:14 — **“And they swear to lies knowingly”**). The Book's answer to their scheme is that the people being deceived were protected by the One they could not deceive, and the community's life went on with a knowledge of them that they had not planned for. The reader is shown a pattern here that repeats in every age: the person who sets out to manage the perceptions of a community usually succeeds for a while, since the community cannot see what is hidden, and the same Book that exposed him at the beginning says that the accounting belongs to God. The difference between the successful plot and the one that collapses is therefore a matter of time, and the Book measures it against a scale the plotter cannot read.

**SCHEME FALLING BACK ON ITS MAKER**

The sentence turns on itself with its next words: ***“yet they only deceive themselves”***. The verb is the same verb used at the start, and the same act is traced back to the one who performed it. The explanation the early teachers gave is that the harm of the plot landed on the plotters: they were exposed in this life and punished in the next, and the gain they hoped for never came. The Book states the same law in a sentence about these very people: (4:142 — **“Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them”**). What follows that sentence in the same place describes their prayer, which they perform lazily and for the eyes of others, and the description fits the men in this passage exactly. That is why the deceit is said to fall back on the deceiver, since the plot has no effect on the One it was aimed at and leaves its mark only on the man who made it. The reader who has ever kept a lie alive to protect a position will recognise the cost, because the lie demands the whole of his attention and gives him nothing in return. A person who lies to a community is not lying to the community; he is choosing a version of himself to live in, and the verse leaves him there with the choice.

**A SHOPSMAN WHO USES A FALSE SCALE**

Think of a trader who buys a scale that shows every weight heavier than it is, and who practises with it until his hand knows the trick. He cheats his customers, and the first man harmed by the arrangement is himself, because he now buys and sells with a mind that cannot tell true weights from false ones. The verse follows the same path with the pretenders, and it finishes by naming the thing they lack: ***“but they fail to perceive it”***. They do not know that the loss is theirs, and the not-knowing is the last stage of the road. These days the same blindness appears whenever a person decides that the truth about him is a thing to be managed, since the management quickly becomes the whole of his life. The sūrah continues by describing the disease that made such a course possible.

---

## Verse 2:10

> There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies

**THE ILLNESS THAT WAS ALREADY IN THE HEART**

The sūrah now names the cause of the behaviour it has described: ***“There is sickness in their hearts”***. The word describes a disorder that weakens a living thing from inside, and the transmitted reading identifies doubt settled where certainty should be. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the sickness as doubt, hypocrisy, disagreement with the truth and darkness, and al-Suddī and others also took it as doubt, while a second line of explanation traces it to a desire that has overcome its owner rather than to a simple lack of information. The two readings belong together, since a doubt that is entertained long enough becomes a desire, and the desire then defends itself against every proof. The early teachers were careful on this point, and they described the sickness as a defect in the heart rather than a weakness in the arguments, because the men being described had every proof in front of them. The men described in the verse did not arrive at their position in a day; the illness was in them, and the events of the sūrah only brought it out.

**THE INCREASE THAT FOLLOWS THE ILLNESS**

The next clause states what happens to a person in that condition: ***“and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase”***. The increase is tied to the revelation itself, since every new verse that came down was a fresh opportunity for the healthy heart and a fresh burden on the sick one. The Book states the same law in another sūrah where a difficult passage is sent and its effect on two groups is described: (9:125 — **“it has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness”**). The Book uses the phrase about the sick heart in several places, and one of them shows the same people arguing about a passage instead of submitting to it: (74:31 — **“those ˹hypocrites˺ with sickness in their hearts and the disbelievers will argue”**). A remedy can become part of the disease for the one who resists it, since the command a healthy person obeys makes a sick person worse by giving him something else to resist. That is why the verse traces the increase to God rather than to the revelation, because the same act is mercy for one heart and judgment for another.

**THE PUNISHMENT AND WHAT IT IS FOR**

The verse finishes with the outcome: ***“They will suffer a painful punishment”***, ***“for their lies”***. The wording gives the reason for the punishment, and the reason is the lie rather than the sickness, which shows that the illness in the heart does not excuse the man who acts on it. In the first generation the phrase was taken as the lie they told with their tongues when they said they believed, and it was also taken as their denial of the messenger, and the two readings describe the same person from different sides. The Book names the same men in another place where their hearts are visible in their faces: (5:52 — **“You see those with sickness in their hearts racing for their guardianship”**). What turns on this verse is that a person's words carry his inner state into the open, so that the hidden illness is not private for long. A community that has been warned about this group can protect itself, and the individual who hears the warning can examine what his own speech has been hiding. The reason the illness is named so plainly here is that a hidden sickness cannot be treated, while a named one can be brought to the physician.

**A WOUND COVERED WITH A CLEAN BANDAGE**

Think of a man who is wounded and who dresses the wound carefully to hide it from his family. The bandage is neat, and the wound is still working under it, quietly and without stopping, until the day the leg can no longer carry him. The verse describes a heart in that condition, and the comparison shows why the sūrah takes the trouble to name the matter in the middle of a description of public behaviour. These days a person can present a disciplined surface while the doubt underneath is fed by everything he reads and watches, and the passage asks him to deal with the illness rather than with the covering. The verses that follow show the same men at work among their neighbours, so its machinery is recognised before it appears.

---

## Verse 2:11

> When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”

**THE COMMAND THEY WERE GIVEN AND THE ANSWER THEY MADE**

The verse records an exchange between the pretenders and the people who corrected them: ***“When they are told”***, ***“Do not spread corruption in the land”***, ***“they reply”***, ***“We are only peace-makers!”***. The command is addressed to a group living inside a community that was being built, and the early teachers explained the corruption as the work that undermines a society from within: teaching doubt, carrying news to the enemy, and holding the believers back from the obligations they had accepted. Ibn ʿAbbās read the phrase as the attempt to turn people away from the religion, and al-Suddī and others read it as the whole of the work that spoils the life of a city, whether by disbelief, by betrayal or by stirring quarrels between neighbours. The command is repeated to every community in every age, and the Book states it as an instruction addressed to the readers of the revelation rather than to a single crowd: (7:56 — **“Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order”**).

**THE SELF-IMAGE THAT SURVIVED THE PROOF**

The answer of the pretenders is a claim about themselves: ***“We are only peace-makers!”***. The wording they chose is a claim to be the repairers rather than the spoilers, and the verse records it without a single word of comment of its own. One of the earliest teachers is reported to have said that these men had not yet appeared in his time, which shows how carefully the community watched for the type the verse describes. The Book records the same self-image in a later sūrah where the pretenders are asked to consider their end, and the question waits for them on the other side of the argument: (47:22 — **“you would then spread corruption throughout the land”**). What the reader is being taught is that a person's own account of his intentions is not evidence about his effect, and the verse puts the proof of the claim outside the claimant's hands. That is why the sūrah does not bother to argue with the sentence they produced, because the argument belongs to the damage and not to the words.

**THE MEASURE THAT IS NOT THE INTENTION**

The sūrah settles the question of measurement in the verse that follows, but the principle is present here already. The pretenders worked for a political result inside a community that had received its law, and the damage they did was measured by the damage itself and not by their intention. The Book elsewhere calls the same activity by its name and adds a verdict that removes the ambiguity: (5:64 — **“And they strive to spread corruption in the land. And Allah does not like corruptors”**). The reason this matters for the reader is that intentions are the last refuge of a person who has made a mess of his effect, and the verse removes the refuge without dismissing the possibility that the man had talked himself into believing his own account. The Book treats the self-image as a real thing in its own right, and it warns about it in a passage that begins with a question about the end of such confidence. What turns on it is the difference between a person who repairs what his work damaged and a person who defends his work because admitting the damage would cost him too much.

**A TENANT WHO CALLS HIS TAMPERING REPAIRS**

Think of a tenant who knocks out a load-bearing wall to make his room brighter and then tells the landlord that he has improved the building. The intention was comfort; the effect is a house that may fall down. The verse gives the community a way of measuring claims about who is helping and who is harming, and it gives the individual a way of measuring himself. These days the same argument is made about institutions and about reputations, where a person can call every act of self-promotion a service to the group. The reader who takes the verse seriously will ask what his behaviour does to the people around him, and he will let that answer settle a question his own account of his motives cannot settle. The correction is not meant to make a person suspicious of every good intention, since the community needs people who build, and it is meant to give him a standard he can check. A person who repairs what he has damaged is on one road, and a person who defends his work because the alternative is an admission is on another, and the difference is decided long before either man says a word about his reasons.

---

## Verse 2:12

> Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it

**FALSE REPAIR EXPOSED**

The sūrah answers the pretenders in a single short verse: ***“Indeed, it is they”***, ***“who are the corruptors”***. The opening word is a particle of alerting, and its force is to make the reader stop and look, since the sentence that follows overturns what the men had just said about themselves. The Book does not argue with them and does not describe their reasons; it states what they are, and the first generations treated the sentence as a verdict on the result of their work rather than on the tone of their speech. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the corruption in question was the blocking of the road to the religion, and Ibn Masʿūd is credited with the same reading, which means the harm was measured by the number of people who were kept away and not by any damage the men intended to do.

**THE WORDS THEY COULD NOT HEAR**

The verse adds why the sentence had to be spoken at all: ***“but they fail to perceive it”***. The phrase repeats almost word for word from the earlier description of the same group, and the repetition is the point, because the men had now been told twice that they were damaging the community. The Book describes their blindness again in another sūrah where their whole way of life is named in a list: (5:64 — **“And they strive to spread corruption in the land. And Allah does not like corruptors”**). The reason the verse returns to the same phrase is that the punishment of the pretender is not only the loss of the reward but the loss of the ability to see what he has done, and the two losses belong together. The failure to see is part of the verdict rather than an excuse for it.

**THE REPAIR THAT IS NOT REPAIR**

The work named in this sentence is worth pinning down for a reader who meets the word often and rarely in a plain sense. The Book uses it for whatever breaks the order God has set in a society: the taking of life, the breaking of agreements, the spreading of falsehood and the poisoning of trust between neighbours. The pretenders of this passage did their damage in the coin of trust, since they spoke as members of the community while carrying the community's affairs to its enemies, and one betrayal of that kind can undo the work of years. The early teachers described the same group as the one whose inside and outside differ, and the corruption follows from the difference itself, because the community cannot protect itself from a man it believes to be its own. That is why the verse does not describe a single act of the men but names their standing among the people, and why the reader is meant to fear the description for himself before he looks for it in anyone else. The Book is careful here in a way that should be noticed, since it never accuses the pretenders of a crime that a court could punish; what it names is the state of a man whose presence in a community is itself the harm.

**A TERMITE THAT LOOKS LIKE A GRAIN OF WOOD**

Think of a beam in a roof that has been eaten hollow from the inside and still wears a sound brown surface to the eye. Nothing on the outside of the timber announces the damage, and the whole roof depends on that beam. The pretender is the beam in the community, and the sūrah tells the reader what he is before it tells him what to do about it. These days the damage of the same kind travels through messages and reputations rather than through arms, and the description holds without any change, because the harm is done by a person the group still counts as one of its own. The verse is short because there is nothing to discuss once the matter has been stated, and the reader is left to decide what he will do with the sentence now that he has heard it. The reason the sentence is placed immediately after the claim of repair is that a claim and its refutation belong together, and the reader who meets them in that order cannot mistake the verdict for a later opinion. The two verses therefore form one movement, and the next exchange between the same people and their neighbours begins on the same footing, with a command and an answer that shows what they really think of the people they live among.

---

## Verse 2:13

> And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know

**AN INSTRUCTION THEY COULD NOT ACCEPT**

The next exchange between the same people and their neighbours begins with an instruction: ***“And when they are told”***, ***“Believe”***, ***“as others believe,”***. The people held up as the standard are the Companions of the Prophet, and the early authorities agree on this: Ibn ʿAbbās named ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions from the Jewish community of Madinah who had accepted the message, and other teachers named the emigrants and the helpers as a body. The command is not to invent a faith of one's own but to take the shape the community had taken, and the reason is that faith is not a private theory about God but a way of living that a person enters alongside others. The Book settles the same point when it describes the people who answered the call and left the most of what they had: they became the standard by which the next generation was measured, and the verse here makes that standard an instruction.

**FOLLY RETURNED TO THE SCOFFERS**

The reply of the pretenders is recorded in their own words: ***“Will we believe”***, ***“as the fools believe?”***. They took the word for foolishness and fixed it to the people who had submitted, and the early teachers explained the answer as the defence of a position rather than a question of fact. The Book uses the same accusation in the story of another prophet, where the chiefs of his people answered him in exactly that tone: (7:66 — **“We surely see you as a fool”**). The pattern is worth noticing for the reason that it repeats: when a person cannot answer the substance of a call, he turns to the character of the people who answered it. That is why the insult is met with a verdict instead of an explanation, since the explanation had already been given and refused. The pretenders could see that the believers had given up comfortable positions and old alliances, and they measured that sacrifice by the standards of the market and found it a loss, which means the insult was really an argument about what a person should count as gain.

**THE REVERSAL THAT THE VERSE PRONOUNCES**

The sūrah takes the word back and gives it to the men who used it: ***“Indeed, it is they”***, ***“who are fools, but they do not know”***. The Book pronounces the verdict in two parts, the second of which explains why the first was needed. A fool in this usage is not a person with a weak mind; he is a person who has the wrong measure of what is worth having, and the Book applies the word on that basis. It states the same judgment about the man who turns away from the way of Abraham: (2:130 — **“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool!”**). The early teachers said that the men knew very well who the people of understanding were, and that they used the word because it served their position, which means the verdict here is about a preference and not about an intellect. What turns on the reversal is that the reader learns where the judgment of worth sits, and it does not sit with the loudest voice in the room.

**A CROWD THAT LAUGHS AT THE FIRST PEOPLE TO BOARD**

Think of a ship being loaded while a crowd on the quay mocks the passengers for giving up their places in the town. The laughter is loud until the water rises, and then the word for foolishness moves to the ones still standing on the shore. The verse uses the same reversal with the community that had accepted the message while the pretenders kept their options open, and the reversal is stated in the language the mockers themselves had used. These days the same scene repeats whenever a person decides that the standards of the people around him are the measure of what is sensible, and the passage gives him the freedom to be counted a fool by that measure while keeping his place among the people who submitted. The ending of the verse settles which of the two groups knows what it is doing, and it leaves the matter there. The reason the passage does not soften the word is that the choice between the two measures is a choice about who a person is, and a softened word would leave the reader free to hold both measures at once.

---

## Verse 2:14

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”

**ONE TONGUE BEFORE TWO COMPANIES**

The verse shows the pretender in the two settings that decide his character: ***“When they meet the believers they say,”***, ***“We believe.”***, ***“But when alone with their evil associates they say,”***, ***“We are definitely with you”***, ***“we were only mocking.”***. The two speeches are given in full and without comment, and the contrast between them is the whole of the lesson. Ibn ʿAbbās named the emigrants and the helpers as the people they greeted with the first sentence, and the leaders of the hostility as the company they spoke to in the second. The verse is a portrait, and the manner of the portrait is worth noticing: the sūrah has not accused the men of a crime, and it lets them convict themselves out of their own mouths. That is why the passage has kept its power in every generation, since the words fit anyone whose company changes the shape of his speech.

**PURPOSE BEHIND THE PUBLIC PROFESSION**

The word they used among the believers is a claim, and the Book reports it as a claim and not as a fact: ***“We believe.”***. The purpose behind the sentence is named in the second half of the verse, where the men describe their own activity in the company of their leaders. The Book states the same behaviour about the same class of people in a later sūrah where their oaths are the subject: (63:2 — **“They have made their ˹false˺ oaths as a shield”**). The wording shows the reason for the shield, which was to keep the advantages of living inside a community while working against it, and the Book leaves the resulting position to the reader's judgment. What turns on the picture is that the pretender's faith is a tool rather than a conviction, and the difference shows itself the moment the two companies are compared.

**THE COMPANY THAT HEARD THE TRUTH**

The second speech is not even a denial of the first, and the men admit their motive inside it: ***“we were only mocking.”***. The Book records the same confession from another group and answers it with a question that closes the door they were trying to slip through: (9:65 — **“Was it Allah, His revelations, and His Messenger that you ridiculed?”**). The reason this verse is placed after the exchanges about belief and corruption is that the reader has now seen the whole machine at work, and the machine ends in mockery of the very thing the men were pretending to accept. The early teachers described the pretenders of this passage as those whose inside is the opposite of their outside, and the two sentences in this verse are the evidence for that description. A community that hears this verse can protect its business from such men, and an individual who hears it can watch his own tongue for the same shift, since flattery in one room and contempt in another is not a complication of faith but its replacement.

**A GUEST WHO PRAISES THE MEAL AND MOCKS THE HOST**

Think of a guest who praises every dish at the table while the host is standing at the door, and who describes the house as a joke in the car on the way home. His praise was not false in the sense of being overheard, and none of it was connected to anything he believed. The verse gives the reader both sides of the same evening, and the comparison is uncomfortable because most people can recognise a moment when their speech bent to fit the company they were in. These days the same man can be found in any workplace or family, agreeing with everyone and belonging to no one, and the sūrah has already given the cure in its first verses by naming the marks of the people whose speech does not change. The verse ends without a threat in it, which is the Book's way of letting a reader draw his own conclusion while the sentence sits inside him.

**BOTH SPEECHES IN ONE VERSE**

The remainder of the passage answers the two speeches with the mockery the men had intended for others, and the answer is delivered in the next verse. The Book holds both sentences in one place for a reason, since the pretender's problem is not one lie but a divided life, and a divided life cannot be described in one place any more than it can be lived in one place. The single verse that carries both conversations makes the division visible in a way that two separate verses would not, and the reader who sees it can no longer pretend that the two speeches belong to two different men. That is why the two sentences are quoted one after the other without a word between them, because the Book wants the reader to hear the same voice in both and to draw the conclusion for himself.

---

## Verse 2:15

> Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance

**MOCKERY MEETS THE DIVINE REPLY**

The verse answers the two-faced speech of the pretenders with a single sentence: ***“Allah will throw their mockery back at them”***. The wording describes the return of a thing to the person who sent it, which means the men are paid in the coin they chose for others. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with a reading in which the return happens at the gate of the Garden, where the pretenders are admitted and then shut out while the believers look on, and the early teachers generally held that the punishment is named after the offence it matches. The Book uses the same sentence about another group of mockers who laughed at the believers for their giving: (9:79 — **“Allah will throw their mockery back at them, and they will suffer a painful punishment”**). The reason the return is traced to God rather than to the believers is that no community is asked to take its own revenge, and the verse lifts the matter to a court that never misses a case.

**THE BLINDNESS THAT CONTINUES IN PLACE**

The sentence finishes with the state the men are left in: ***“leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance”***. The wording describes a walk with no direction and a stubborn refusal to stop, and the condition is described as continuing rather than beginning here. The Book uses the same phrase at the end of a passage about people whose hearts were turned away from the truth: (6:110 — **“leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance”**). The repetition is deliberate, because the verse is telling the reader that the punishment of this group is the road they had already chosen, now extended and made permanent. The phrase was taken by the first generation as a description of men who cannot tell faith from error any longer, which means the blindness is not a lack of light but the loss of the ability to use it. The warning here is about the seriousness of a habit that is defended long enough, since a road that begins as a preference can end as a condition, and the man who chose it no longer has the freedom he thought he was protecting.

**MOCKERY AS A FORM OF OPEN DEFIANCE**

A reader may wonder why the Book treats mockery as a crime heavy enough for this answer, and the reason is in what mockery does to a community. Ridicule is the cheapest way to make a person ashamed of a good he had decided to do, and it costs the mocker nothing while it empties the work of the people he laughs at. The Book names the same weapon in the hands of the men of the past and says that the reckoning reached them too: (45:35 — **“you made a mockery of Allah's revelations”**). The pretenders of this sūrah used their two speeches to keep their position, and when the position was threatened they laughed at the faith of the people who fed them and sheltered them. That is why the answer comes from God and lands on the mockery itself, and why the reader is meant to be careful with a joke about another person's worship, since the Book keeps a record of it.

**A BALL THROWN AGAINST A WALL**

Think of a boy who throws a ball at a wall to frighten someone on the other side and finds the ball coming back at his own face. The verse uses the same image of return, and the comparison helps a reader see why the sentence is a fitting answer rather than a random punishment. These days a person can destroy a reputation with a laugh, and the platform carries the joke further than the intention ever travelled, which is the mockery of this verse with a longer reach. The reader is given the choice of the company he joins, and the sūrah has already said which company keeps its word. A community cannot arrest every mocker and should not try, and the verse reassures the people who are laughed at that the matter is not left unfinished anywhere, in this life or beyond it. The next verse turns to the two roads this traffic has been moving between, and it shows what a person loses when he chooses the one the mockers took.

---

## Verse 2:16

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE TRADE THAT IS NAMED IN THE BOOK'S OWN TERMS**

The next verse gathers the whole passage into one image and describes the pretenders as traders: ***“They are the ones”***, ***“who trade guidance for misguidance.”***. The image is exact, and it means that the men had something of value in their hands and exchanged it for something worthless. Ibn ʿAbbās read the guidance as the clear road the message had brought them and the misguidance as the error they preferred, and al-Suddī and Qatādah likewise saw a knowing exchange. The Book uses the same figure for the people who were given a share of the Scripture and sold it: (4:44 — **“trade it for misguidance”**), and it uses it again for those who gave belief for disbelief in a later sūrah. What turns on the image is that the men are not described as ignorant of the value of what they held, since a trader knows what he is carrying, and their fault is the price they accepted.

**THE PROFIT THAT NEVER ARRIVED**

The sentence follows the trade to its ledger: ***“But this trade is profitless”***. The word describes a bargain in which nothing is gained, and the verse states the outcome as a fact rather than as a threat. The Book names the same transaction in another place and adds what the traders kept in place of what they sold: (2:175 — **“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment”**). The men in the passage did not lose something theoretical, since what they gave up was a road, a community and a destination, and the verse states plainly that the exchange produced nothing at all. That is why the sūrah does not present the pretenders as enviable, whatever the appearance of their position, because a trade with no profit leaves the trader where he started and poorer for the effort.

**THE GUIDANCE THEY NO LONGER HAVE**

The verse closes with the second half of the loss: ***“and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided”***. The sentence does not say that they will be guided later; it places them outside the description for the present, and the Book uses the same verdict in a passage about people who gave up belief for its opposite: (3:177 — **“Those who trade belief for disbelief will never harm Allah in the least”**). The wording also settles a question that a reader might carry about the men's sincerity, since a person who has made the exchange and knows it is not a person who is still looking. The early teachers explained the phrase as the loss of the direction that the Book gives to anyone who comes to it honestly, which means the guidance was available and refused. A man who has walked a road and then chosen another is not in the position of a man who has never seen the first, and the verse treats the difference as the whole of the matter. What follows in the sūrah is a pair of pictures that show how such a person ends up walking, and the reader meets the first of them in the next verse.

**A TRADER WHO SWAPS A PLOUGH FOR A BROKEN LAMP**

Think of a farmer who trades his plough for a lamp with no oil, and who defends the bargain in front of the neighbours because he has already made it. The verse describes a decision of that shape and follows it to the field left unploughed and the dark room where the lamp was meant to serve. These days the same bargain is made whenever a person sets aside a practice or a conviction for something that cannot carry him through a hard season, and the sūrah's plain account of profit and loss saves him from the salesmanship of the moment. The reader is asked to look at what he is holding and to ask what he traded for it, and the answer to that question is the beginning of the road back. The sūrah does not leave him with the picture alone, and what follows is a second picture that shows the same man in a storm, which is where every trade of this kind is finally tested.

---

## Verse 2:17

> Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see

**FIRE KINDLED THEN TAKEN AWAY**

The sūrah now sets the whole passage in a picture: ***“Their example is that of someone”***, ***“who kindles a fire”***. The image is a man in the dark who lights a fire, sees the ground around him and feels safe, and then loses the light in a single moment. The first readers of the passage applied every part of the picture with care. Ibn ʿAbbās described a man who lit the fire to protect his family and property, and who saw what surrounded him and felt secure just before the flame went out, and he compared that to the pretenders whose safety and standing came from their public profession. Al-Suddī and others added that the fire was borrowed rather than owned, which is why it could be taken away without the man losing anything of his own. The picture is placed after the verse about the trade, and the placing is deliberate, since the loss of the light is the visible form of the loss described in the ledger. A reader who has just been shown a bargain with no profit is now shown the man who made it standing in the dark, and the second image is meant to be remembered with the first.

**THE MOMENT THE LIGHT IS TAKEN**

The middle of the verse holds the reversal: ***“but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness”***. The wording does not say that the fire went out by itself, and it does not say that the man put it out, since the sentence traces the act to God. That is the point of the picture for a reader who wonders why the pretenders were not exposed and punished at once: the light was given for a term, and the term belonged to the One who gave it. The Book shows the same scene at the end of the road in a sūrah where the pretenders ask the believers for a share of their light: (57:13 — **“Wait for us so that we may have some of your light.”**). Those men had lived by a borrowed light in this world without owning it, and the scene shows what happens when the borrowing ends. What turns on the picture is that a person's standing in a community is not the same thing as his standing before God.

**THE CONDITION THE PICTURE LEAVES BEHIND**

The verse closes with the state of the man in the dark: ***“unable to see”***. The early teachers read the phrase as confusion about the way and fear of what surrounds him, since a person in darkness cannot move and cannot defend himself. The Book uses light and darkness for the two conditions of the heart in a verse that contrasts them directly: (6:122 — **“a light with which they can walk among people”**). The difference between the two is the difference between walking and standing still, and the pretender who has lost his light is described as a man who cannot take a step. The reason the sūrah uses a picture instead of a verdict here is that the reader can hold the image longer than he holds a sentence, and it is the image that comes back to him when he is tempted to let his public face get ahead of his private state.

**A CAMPER WHO BORROWED A LANTERN**

Think of a man who sets out across a field at night carrying a lantern he borrowed from a neighbour, and who plans his route by its light while saying nothing about where the lantern came from. The light serves him for as long as the owner allows it, and the moment it is taken back the field is exactly what it was before. The picture fits the pretenders because their light was never theirs, and it fits the reader who is honest about his own dependence, since everything he sees by is given to him. These days a person can build a whole reputation out of a light that belongs to a community rather than to himself, and the verse quietly asks whose the lantern is. What follows is the second picture, which handles the kind of pretender who is not left standing in the dark but is carried along by forces he cannot control.

---

## Verse 2:18

> They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺

**THE THREE SENSES THE PICTURE LEAVES CLOSED**

Three closed faculties draw the condition in a single portrait: ***“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb”***, ***“and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺”***. The wording names the three instruments a person uses to receive the truth, to speak it and to follow it, and it closes all three. Ibn ʿAbbās read the description as men who made themselves deaf, dumb and blind, and the early teachers generally understood the three as a description of deliberate refusal rather than of physical defect. The Book uses the same three for people whose faculties were given and then left unused, and it adds a comparison that removes any doubt about the fault: (7:179 — **“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with”**). The three instruments are named instead of the men so that the reader tests his own use of them, since the danger is not the absence of the equipment but its disuse.

**CHOSEN DEAFNESS AND ITS END**

The translation carries the sense that the deafness here is a willed condition, and another sūrah states the same thing with the same word: (6:39 — **“Those who deny Our signs are ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb—lost in darkness”**). The wording matters because it answers a complaint that a person may raise about his own hardness: the Book does not describe a man who was never given ears, and it describes a man who turned them off. The mute part of the description was explained as the inability to speak of anything good, which means the silence is not modesty but the loss of the tongue's first purpose. What turns on the distinction is that a person still carries the ability while he refuses the use, and the refusal is a decision that is made again every time the truth arrives. The Book never describes a person as beyond hearing while he is still able to hear, and the verse leaves the door where it found it.

**THE END OF THE ROAD IN THE LAST WORDS**

The sentence closes with a verdict about return: ***“they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺”***. The wording describes a turning back to a place a person has left, and it says the turning will not happen. The Book states the same outcome for people who have blinded the instruments of their hearts and adds the reason they cannot see: (22:46 — **“it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind”**). The phrase was understood as a description of a settled direction rather than a decree about a person who still intends to turn, and the difference between the two readings matters to anyone who fears for a relative. The verse describes the ones who have been fully described already in the passage, and it does not give the community a licence to write anyone off while he is alive.
