The pairing is deliberate, because a person who is convinced that God is everywhere might still wonder whether his act in a strange place counts, and the second name settles that question. The Book frequently closes a statement about God's ownership with an attribute that covers the reader's practical worry, and the two words here do exactly that. What the sentence establishes is that the whole dispute about places was settled the moment its true owner was named, and the names that follow make the settlement personal. Today, travel and displacement can remove familiar surroundings without placing a worshipper beyond the ownership, knowledge or nearness of God.

---

## Verse 2:116

> They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will

**CREATOR AND CREATURE CONFUSED BY DESCENT**

A claim about God is reported here that the Book treats as a category error rather than a difference of opinion, and it is stated in two words: ***“They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him!”***. The claim is quoted without its authors being named, which places the sentence beside the disputes of the earlier verses as one more assertion made about God without warrant. The Book's answer begins immediately with the words of exaltation rather than with an argument, and the order tells the reader that the claim is being refused at its root. The communities that made such claims had scriptures and traditions, and the verse shows the reader what can be said about God by people who have both. What follows in the sentence is the reasoning that the exaltation only begins. Ibn ʿAbbās connected the claim of a son with what was said about Ezra and Jesus, then read the answer as universal servitude that leaves no creature outside God's ownership.

**EXALTATION BEFORE ARGUMENT**

The phrase of exaltation is the Book's standard reply when a claim about God is too small for its subject, and its placement here is a judgement on the claim before any evidence is offered. The words describe God as free of every deficiency, and among the deficiencies is the suggestion that He shares His nature with anything. Other passages answer the reported claim of offspring with identical exaltation, and in one of them the exaltation is followed by the same kind of reasoning used here: (19:35 — **“It is not for Allah to take a son!”**). The reader is therefore shown a pattern the Book follows consistently, where the claim is refused by a statement about what God is rather than by a comparison between God and the claimants. A person who has heard a doctrine about God that struck him as unworthy of the subject will recognise the reply.

**UNIVERSAL OWNERSHIP ANSWERS THE CLAIM**

The verse then gives the reason the claim collapses, and the reason is about ownership: ***“In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens”***, ***“and the earth”*** and ***“all are subject to His Will”***. A person who owns everything cannot have derived a part of himself from it, since ownership and derivation are different relations and the verse keeps them apart. The same claim about ownership appears in a passage that also reports the claim of a son, and the order of the two statements there matches the order here: (6:101 — **“How could He have children when He has no mate?”**). The Book's argument is not that the claim is unlikely but that it is incoherent, since the one who owns all things has nothing beside Him from which anything could be begotten. The sentence therefore rests on a fact the reader has already met many times in the sūrah.

**A CRAFTSMAN WHO OWNS HIS WORK**

Think of a craftsman whose work fills a workshop and who is said to have fathered the furniture he made, so that the relation between him and his work is confused with the relation between him and a child. The verse's reasoning separates the two, and it does so by naming the whole created order as his possession. The comparison makes plain why the Book treats the claim as an error about God's nature rather than as an insult, since the mistake lies in the kind of relation that is being asserted. Anyone who has heard a person speak of the divine in terms drawn from human families can see how easily the confusion arises, and how simply the Book dissolves it. What the sentence leaves with the reader is the ownership of everything and the subordination of everything, which together rule out the claim.

**SUBJECTION AS THE STATE OF EVERYTHING**

The verse ends with a clause that goes beyond ownership to describe the condition of the created order: all are subject to His Will. The word describes a readiness to be directed, and it is applied here to everything in the heavens and the earth without exception. Closing a refutation with a statement about the created order shows the reader the scale of what is being discussed when a claim about God is made. The sentence declares God free of the deficiency, states that everything belongs to Him, and describes everything as under His command. The next verse names Him as the one who originated the heavens and the earth, which places the same reasoning in a sentence about creation itself. In the present day, admiration becomes corruption when a servant of God is lifted from honoured service into a share of divine identity.

---

## Verse 2:117

> ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is

**THE ORIGINATOR NAMED FIRST**

God is now named as the One who brought the heavens and earth into being, directly answering the previous sentence, and the name chosen describes invention rather than assembly: ***“˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens”*** and ***“and the earth!”***. The term used belongs to the vocabulary of creating something without a prior model, which is the answer to a claim about offspring in two ways: the originator is not the father of what he originates, and what he originates owes him everything. The Book's argument in the previous verse rested on ownership, and this sentence supplies the ground of that ownership by naming the act that produced it. The sequence has now supplied the reason the claim cannot stand: an originator and what He originates do not share the relation of parent and child. What the reader receives here is a title rather than an argument, and the title settles the matter. Ibn ʿAbbās read the originator as the One who brought the heavens and earth from nothing, and the command to be as sufficient even for creating Jesus without a father.

**DECREE DESCRIBED IN A SINGLE WORD**

The sentence then describes how this originator acts when he decides something: ***“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!”***. The contrast with the claim of the previous verse is exact, since the Book has just denied that God has offspring and now shows how everything that exists came to be: by a command. No intermediary, no partner and no material is named, and the absence is the whole content of the clause. Another sūrah states the same principle in similar words, and it also draws the conclusion that a child is impossible for such a maker: (40:68 — **“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it”**). The Book uses this sentence wherever it needs to establish that creation depends on God's word alone, which is why it appears in the answers to several claims about divine sonship. A reader who has understood the clause has understood why the claim of the previous verse could not survive.

**DECREE WITHOUT PROCESS OR DELAY**

The command is quoted in the verse itself, and the sentence closes with the result following immediately on the word: ***“And it is”***. The Book places no interval between the decree and the existence of what is decreed, and the two words that end the sentence carry the whole of its force. The same pair of words describes the coming into being of a child in the annunciation to Mary, where the impossibility is answered in exactly this form. The use of so short a sentence for so large a claim is deliberate, since the Book's manner in these verses is to state the ease of the act rather than to describe its mechanics. The picture left behind is one of a command that is not followed by effort.

**A BUILDER WHO SPEAKS THE HOUSE INTO PLACE**

Think of a builder who does not lay a single brick but describes a house and finds it standing where he spoke of it. The verse's clause about the decree works at a larger scale and with no comparison intended, since the point of the image is that the result has no relation to labour. The comparison also makes clear why the two sentences of this passage belong together: the one denies that God has a family, and the other shows that what exists came to be without the involvement that a family would imply. Anyone who has watched a person try to account for the world without a maker can see how much the Book's answer depends on this single clause. What the verse offers is not an explanation of creation but the plainest statement of who created.

**THE PAIR OF VERSES AND WHAT THEY SETTLE**

Read together, the two sentences answer the claim of offspring in two stages, and each stage removes a different part of it. The ownership of everything rules out the possibility of a derived divine nature, and the command that produces everything rules out the need for any such derivation in the first place. The Book's practice in these verses is to answer a doctrinal claim with a statement about God's relation to the created order, and the two statements here are as brief as any in the sūrah. A reader who wanted a longer argument has the short one to work with, since the sentence about the decree leaves nothing for a partner to do. What remains for the reader is the title with which the passage opened, and the ease with which the Book has disposed of the claim. Today, human production depends on materials, time and failed attempts, while the verse preserves the absolute difference between manufacture and creation.

---

## Verse 2:118

> Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith

**THE DEMAND TO HEAR GOD SPEAK**

The verse puts a demand into the mouths of the people who had no scripture, and it quotes them directly: ***“Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us”*** and ***“or a sign would come to us!”***. The demand is not for a clearer argument but for a different kind of communication, one in which the audience sets the terms. The Book has spent several verses answering claims made by communities with scriptures, and it now turns to the party that had no book at all and shows that the same demand was in its mouth. The phrasing is important because it places the condition on God rather than on the hearers, as though the message could only be accepted if it arrived by the route they had chosen. The demand on display is one that would not have settled anything, since it asks for a sign whose terms are dictated by the people who would have to accept it. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the ignorant demand as a request for direct divine speech or a fresh sign, and the likeness of hearts as recurrence of the same refusal among earlier generations.

**THE OLD DEMAND IN NEW MOUTHS**

The sentence then connects the demand to an older history, and the connection is the answer: ***“The same was said by those”*** and ***“who came before. Their hearts are all alike.”***. The Book's argument is about resemblance rather than about chronology, and the clause about the hearts states the reason the same words keep appearing in different centuries. Another sūrah records the demand in the mouth of the community that received Moses, where the request for a sign was followed by the same refusal as before: (6:124 — **“We will never believe until we receive what Allah’s messengers received”**). The repetition is offered as evidence that the demand does not arise from the case being made but from a condition of the heart, and the sentence states that condition in four words. Anyone who has watched the same objection surface in every generation has the sentence to explain it.

**HEARTS THAT CAME OUT ALIKE**

The clause about the hearts is the hinge of the verse, because it moves the discussion from the evidence to the people who are examining it. The Book treats the heart as the place where a decision about a message is taken, and sameness of heart explains the repetition of speech. Another passage records the demand as it was made to Moses' community, and it shows how quickly a request for direct communication turns into a rehearsal of an old complaint: (10:20 — **“Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?”**). The sentence's refusal to describe the demanders as stupid is notable, since it places the problem in a disposition rather than in an intellect. Someone who recognises his own capacity for that disposition will find the clause more useful than an insult would have been.

**A WELL THAT TASTES THE SAME IN EVERY VILLAGE**

Think of a family that has moved through four different towns and found the water in each of them bitter, and that blames the towns. The verse tells the reader that the same complaint has been made in every generation, and it places the cause in the hearts that carried the complaint from place to place. The comparison also illuminates why the Book does not answer the demand with a demonstration, since a demonstration is what the demanders asked for and did not want. A person who finds fault with every offered alternative displays the pattern described here, which does not arise from the alternatives. The unchanged dissatisfaction identifies the heart as the source. The point is that the issue has never been the availability of the signs.

**THE SIGNS MADE CLEAR FOR THE SURE**

The verse closes by stating what has been provided instead, and the statement is unqualified: ***“Indeed, We have made the signs clear”*** and ***“for people of sure faith”***. The signs are described as clear without a condition, and the qualification falls on the people to whom they are clear, which places the difficulty on the receiving side. The particular phrase used here for sure faith describes a confidence that does not wait for further evidence, and the Book treats that confidence as the condition of seeing what is already there. Another sūrah makes the same link between the clarity of the revelation and the people who recognise it: (45:20 — **“a guide and mercy for people of sure faith”**). The sūrah has used this contrast from its opening verses, where the same clarity is placed against the same kind of heart, and the verse here repeats the pattern at the close of an argument. What remains with the reader is the offer of the signs and the phrase that describes those who see them. Present-day scepticism can keep moving the required sign after every clear answer, revealing that the obstacle lies in the terms imposed by the demander.

---

## Verse 2:119

> We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire

**THE TRUTH THE MESSENGER WAS SENT WITH**

The attention moves from the demands of the audience to the description of the one who brought the message, and his commission is stated in three parts: ***“We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺”***, ***“as a deliverer of good news”*** and ***“and a warner.”***. The truth is named as what the sending carried, which places the message rather than the messenger's person at the centre of the sentence. The two roles that follow describe what the truth does when it reaches people: it announces something to those who accept it and warns those who do not. The preceding sentence has just described an audience whose hearts all came out alike, and this sentence answers that scene by describing the work that continues regardless. What the reader receives is a picture of a mission that does not depend on the response it meets. Ibn ʿAbbās joined the truth to the Qur'an and divine oneness, the good news to the Garden, and the warning to the Fire, while treating the final clause as release from responsibility for those who refuse.

**GOOD NEWS AND WARNING AS ONE OFFICE**

The pairing of the two roles is not a division of labour between two messengers but a description of a single office, and the Book uses the pair together whenever it summarises a prophet's work. The good news comes first, which is worth noticing, since the warning is not the whole of what the messenger carries or even most of it. Another sūrah makes the same point when it lists what the earlier messengers brought and what they met: (3:184 — **“so too were messengers before you who came with clear proofs”**). The Book's habit of naming both roles together is a way of saying that the message is complete in what it offers and complete in what it threatens, so that no hearer can claim he was told only half. A reader who has heard the message described only as judgement will find the order of the words here worth his attention.

**THE MESSENGER NOT ANSWERABLE FOR THE OTHERS**

The sentence then relieves the messenger of a burden that the previous verses could easily have placed on him: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** and ***“for the residents of the Hellfire”***. The Book states this as a fact about the mission rather than as a comfort offered to a discouraged man, and the statement follows the description of the office directly. The same assurance appears in the history of the earlier messengers, whose audiences mocked them while the messengers delivered what they had been given: (36:30 — **“No messenger ever came to them without being mocked”**). The division of responsibility runs between the delivery and the response, and only the first belongs to the messenger. A reader who carries a message to people who will not hear it has the sentence as the limit of his obligation.

**A HERALD WHO DOES NOT OWE THE CITY ITS ANSWER**

Think of a herald who rides through a town reading the proclamation and who is not asked afterwards whether the townspeople agreed with it. The verse describes the prophet's work in the same terms, and it names the two directions the proclamation can take without making either of them the messenger's responsibility. The comparison is useful because the pressure a messenger feels is usually about results, and the sentence here removes results from the account. Anyone who has tried to make another person believe something for his own good knows the exhaustion the verse is lifting, and the lifting is done in a single clause. What remains with the messenger is the delivery, which is the part he was given to do.

**THE DELIVERY AND THE RESPONSE**

Read with the verses around it, this sentence explains why the Book can describe an audience that refused and still call the sending a sending. The signs were made clear for people of sure faith, the demand for a different kind of proof was refused, and the messenger is told that the residents of the Fire are not his to answer for. The three statements together form the answer to the objection recorded in the previous verse, and the answer is about the nature of the mission rather than about the objectors' standing. The Book's restraint here is part of its method, since it leaves the outcome with God and the delivery with the messenger. Anyone who has wondered how a prophet could continue after so much refusal has the sentence as the Book's own account of it. Today, a teacher of truth must deliver hope and warning faithfully without treating every hearer's final choice as a personal failure. The reason the Messenger is released from the fate of the Fire's people is that faithful delivery and forced acceptance are different responsibilities.

---

## Verse 2:120

> Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah

**A SATISFACTION THAT WILL NEVER COME**

The verse states a limit that the community had to accept, and it states it in the form of a prediction: ***“Never will the Jews”*** and ***“or Christians be pleased with you”***, followed by ***“until you follow their faith.”***. The two communities are named together again, as they were in the dispute over Paradise, and the sentence explains an experience the believers had been living through. The Book's wording is absolute, and the condition attached to it shows what would have been required: not better conduct, not clearer argument, but the adoption of the others' religion. The sentence is therefore a description of the terms rather than a complaint about the parties, and the terms are of a kind that a believing community cannot meet. What the sentence removes is the expectation that a certain kind of effort will eventually produce approval. Ibn ʿAbbās identified the competing pressures as the religion and prayer-direction of the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran, neither of which could replace revealed guidance.

**THE GUIDANCE NAMED AS ALLAH'S OWN**

The verse supplies the reply the Messenger is to give, and the reply declines the offered terms by naming what he already has: ***“Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.”*** and ***“And”***. The sentence does not enter into a comparison between the two faiths; it states that guidance is a gift from God rather than a possession of a community. The same phrase appears elsewhere in the Book where the claim of belonging is being corrected, which shows how fixed the formula was: (3:73 — **“Surely, ˹the only˺ true guidance is Allah’s guidance”**). Placing this statement immediately after the prediction gives the reader the reason the community could not be satisfied by anything short of conversion: what was at stake was not the approval of the neighbours but the source of the guidance itself. A reader who has been asked to soften a position merely to keep the peace will recognise the reply.

**THE DESIRES THAT WOULD LEAD AWAY**

The verse then addresses a possibility that would never have arisen in a straightforward reading, and it warns against it in the strongest form: ***“if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”***, ***“that has come to you, there would be none to protect”*** and ***“or help you against Allah”***. The warning is given to the Messenger, which addresses the community that follows him, and the words carry the weight of the whole sūrah's argument about what has been received. Another passage states the same danger in a general form, where obedience to the majority is shown to lead away from the path: (6:116 — **“If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way”**). What the Book says about the pressure to conform does not change here, since the danger it names is the desires of other people rather than their arguments.

**TWO HOUSES AND A FENCE THAT CANNOT BE MOVED**

Think of a household whose neighbours will not be satisfied until it moves in with them, and which is asked to give up its kitchen to keep the street quiet. The verse describes a demand of that shape, and it refuses the concession without pretending that the neighbours will change their minds. The comparison is useful because it separates two things a reader easily confuses: being pleasant to one's neighbours and being absorbed by them. Anyone who has seen a conviction given up in small instalments to keep a relationship calm can see what the warning is aimed at, and the warning is not about hostility but about drift. What the verse leaves with the reader is the knowledge of what the pressure is for.

**STEADINESS WITHOUT UNIVERSAL APPROVAL**

The verse ends with the removal of every other protector, so that the community is left with no fallback if it yields. The sūrah has already spoken of the east and the west belonging to God, and the same ownership is stated here as the reason no help exists outside Him. The sentence therefore closes the discussion of the neighbours' approval by placing the community's security entirely with God, which is the answer to the fear that refusing them would leave the believers alone. A reader who has taken the sentence seriously knows what he is choosing when he keeps a conviction under pressure, and he knows whom he is choosing instead. The next verse describes the community that had received the same scripture and held to it, which supplies the contrast the passage has been building. In the present day, public approval remains an endless target because groups with incompatible demands cannot all be pleased by one surrendered conscience.

---

## Verse 2:121

> Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers

**RECITATION PROVED BY LOYAL CONDUCT**

The verse describes a group inside the communities that possessed scriptures, and it does so by what they do rather than by what they are called: ***“Those We have given the Book follow it”*** and ***“as it should be followed. It is they”*** who ***“who ˹truly˺ believe in it.”***. The phrase about following as it should be followed describes a manner of reading rather than a quantity of reading, and the Book's wording makes the manner the standard. The verses just before this one described communities that would not be satisfied until the believers joined them, and this sentence points to the people within those same communities who had done the opposite. The verse therefore prevents the reader from turning the previous sentence into a verdict on everyone who inherited a scripture. What the reader is given is a description that any holder of a book can test himself against. Ibn ʿAbbās read right recitation as preserving the Scripture's lawful and unlawful, command and prohibition, acting on its clear teaching and believing its difficult passages without alteration.

**FOLLOWING A BOOK PROPERLY**

The Book's understanding of following is practical rather than ceremonial, and the verse's two-word standard leaves the reader to work out what it involves. A book is followed properly when its commands are carried out, its warnings are taken seriously, and its claims are not reshaped to fit the reader's preferences. Earlier verses in this passage described communities that recited their scriptures while hiding what they contained, and the contrast here is with people who read and comply. Another passage describes the same group in terms of their conduct at night, which gives the reader a picture of what the phrase looks like in a life: (3:113 — **“Yet they are not all alike: there are some among the People of the Book who are upright”**). The point is that the failure described earlier in the sūrah was never a failure of access to the text.

**BELIEF THAT FOLLOWS FROM READING**

The sentence then attaches belief to the practice, and the attachment runs in the order of the clause: those who follow the book as it should be followed are the ones who believe in it. The Book's treatment of belief as the fruit of obedience is worth noticing, since it puts the two in a sequence rather than in a competition. The same link between studying a scripture and accepting it appears in the description of the scholars who judged by what they had been given: (5:44 — **“So too did the rabbis and scholars judge according to Allah’s Book”**). A reader who has met the idea that belief is a feeling that precedes any practice will find the verse's order instructive, since the Book makes the practice part of the belief rather than a result of it.

**A MUSICIAN WHO PLAYS WHAT IS WRITTEN**

Think of a musician who plays the score in front of him instead of the tune he would have preferred, and who is therefore trusted with the whole repertoire. The verse's phrase about following a book as it should be followed works at that level of fidelity, and the Book treats the difference between the two kinds of reader as decisive. The comparison also explains why the verse can speak of belief in the same breath, since a person who follows what he has been given has already accepted its authority. Anyone who has watched a text being quietly adjusted to suit its reader can see what the phrase is protecting, and the protection is the text itself. The plain question left with him is whether the book he holds is being obeyed or managed.

**REJECTION AND WHAT IT COSTS**

The verse closes with the other group stated in the same terms and with the opposite outcome: ***“As for those who reject it, it is they”*** who ***“who are the losers”***. The symmetry is exact, since the two halves of the sentence use the same construction and place the difference in what the people do with the book. The word for the losers describes a loss measured against what was available rather than against what was expected, the Book's usual description of those who had a scripture in their hands. The sentence therefore ends the passage about the People of the Book with a division that runs through their own ranks rather than between them and everyone else. Possessing a text has plainly never been the same thing as being governed by it. Today, reading a sacred text rightly includes honest transmission and obedient practice, not fluency that leaves conduct untouched.

---

## Verse 2:122

> O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others

**AN ADDRESS THAT REOPENS THE HISTORY**

The verse turns back to the community whose story has run through the sūrah, addressing it by the name that carries its ancestry: ***“O Children of Israel!”***. The address is not a new topic but a return, since the same call has already opened a passage earlier in the chapter where a covenant and its terms were named. The Book's habit of returning to a community after long stretches of other material is part of its method, and the return here comes immediately after a sentence about those who follow their book and those who reject it. The reader is therefore invited to hear the call as the beginning of an argument rather than as a fresh introduction. What the verse asks of the community is stated in the two clauses that follow, and the two clauses are about memory and about a favour.

**REMEMBERING A FAVOUR**

The first request is that the community recall what it had been given: ***“Remember My favours upon you”***. The Book's instruction to remember is not an appeal to nostalgia but a summons to account for the obligations that came with the favours, since the two clauses that follow in the sūrah's earlier passage join memory to a covenant. The sūrah has already named several of these favours, from the deliverance at the sea to the provision in the desert, and the verse's brevity assumes the reader has them in view. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with the view that the remembering here means acting on what the favours require rather than reciting them. What the reader should see is the Book's insistence that a gift received and forgotten is a gift that will be accounted for, since memory is placed first and treated as a duty.

**HONOUR ABOVE THE OTHERS**

The second clause states the particular favour that the community was most likely to remember with pride: ***“and how I honoured you above the others”***. The honouring is stated as a fact here, and the fact is placed beside the command to remember, which keeps it attached to its obligations. The favoured status was real, and the Book nowhere denies it; what it denies is the conclusion the community drew from it in later generations. The comparison with the earlier passage makes the intention clear, since the same words there are followed by the warning of a day on which no soul will be of use to another: (2:47 — **“how I honoured you above the others”**). Someone who has received an advantage and treated it as a possession will find the pairing of favour with duty familiar from his own experience.

**A FAMILY HEIRLOOM WITH A CONDITION ATTACHED**

Think of a family that was given land by a benefactor and that still speaks of the gift while ignoring the terms on which it was made. The verse calls the community back to the memory of the gift, and the Book's method is to name the gift and the terms together so that the second cannot be separated from the first. The comparison explains the Book's frequent returns to this history, since a community that remembers only the favour misunderstands both the favour and itself. Anyone who has inherited an advantage and treated it as an entitlement can see what the sentence is guarding against, and the guard is set at the point of memory. The obligation attached to what he has been given is what the reader is left holding.

**THE RETURN TO AN OLDER HISTORY**

The return to the Children of Israel comes at a point where the sūrah has been discussing the People of the Book, and the two communities are not the same, since the earlier history belongs to a nation rather than to a pair of religious bodies. The Book's argument with this community is about a covenant and a favour, while its argument with the others has been about a scripture and a claim. What the return establishes is that the sūrah's case rests on a history that its first audience knew in detail, and the call by name is a way of placing that history in front of them. Another passage states the same favour in the language of giving and provision, which shows how the Book frames the whole account: (45:16 — **“We gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood”**). The reader who follows the address to its conclusion will find that the favours named are the ground of everything the chapter has been arguing about. Present-day privilege is remembered properly only when gratitude becomes responsibility rather than a claim of permanent superiority.

---

## Verse 2:123

> And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given

**A DAY WITH NO SUBSTITUTES**

The verse completes the call to the Children of Israel with a warning that looks past their history to the day it ends, and the warning is given as an instruction to protect themselves: ***“And guard yourselves against the Day”***. The Book's pattern in these passages is to name the obligations and then to name the accounting, so that the command to remember is followed by the reason the remembering matters. The verse is very close in wording to an earlier sentence in the sūrah that made the same point with a slightly different order, which suggests that the warning was meant to be heard more than once. The whole address is framed by this sentence, since the favours described in it were given to a people who will stand before their giver. Anyone who treats a gift as a private possession has the sentence as the correction it needs. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the Day as one on which neither parent nor child can remove another's sentence, and no ransom, intercessor or helper can overturn the account.

**EVERY ACCOUNT STANDS ALONE**

The first clause of the warning removes the assistance on which a person usually relies: ***“when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted”***. The three refusals come together and close off the three routes by which a person might hope to escape the consequences of his record. The Book states the same three refusals elsewhere in the sūrah, which shows how central the point is to its account of the day: (2:48 — **“Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another”**). Nothing here suggests that the day will be harsh in an undifferentiated way; the exact supports that will be missing are named one by one. A reader who has arranged his affairs around the influence of others has the clause as a plain description of what that arrangement is worth there.

**RANSOM THAT WILL NOT BE TAKEN**

The middle refusal concerns payment, and the Book has something to say about what a ransom would look like if it were possible. Another passage describes a rich man on that day offering everything he owns twice over in exchange for his own release, and the offer is refused at the outset: (39:47 — **“they would certainly offer it to ransom themselves from the horrible punishment on Judgment Day”**). The same image appears in a sūrah where the ransom is measured in gold sufficient to fill the earth, and the answer there is identical: (3:91 — **“it would never be accepted from them”**). The verse's brevity assumes those pictures, and the reader who has them in mind will hear the refusal as the closing of a door. The instruction then adds its own last phrase to the list, and the phrase completes the account of what will not be available: ***“and no help will be given”***.

**A DEBTOR WITH NO FRIENDS IN THE ROOM**

Think of a man brought before a court who has spent his life relying on the standing of his relatives and the goodwill of his neighbours, and who discovers that the room contains only himself and the record. The verse's three refusals strip a person of exactly those supports, and the refusals come in the order a desperate man would try them. The comparison is useful because it shows that the verse is not describing cruelty but accuracy, since each refused route was a route that only worked in the world. Anyone who has seen a person spend his last means on the hope of a favour has seen how the reasoning goes, and the answer here is that the accounting is not a negotiation. What the sentence leaves behind is the sole remaining resource, which is the record a person carries.

**THE GUARDING THE VERSE ASKS FOR**

The instruction is to guard, which means the warning is meant to be acted on now rather than feared later, and the same word the Book uses for keeping away from what is forbidden carries the instruction here. The sūrah has just described people who follow their book as it should be followed and people who reject it, and this sentence tells the reader where the difference shows itself: in the precautions he takes while the day is still ahead of him. The children of Israel had been reminded of favours that came with obligations, and the guarding named here is the form those obligations take when the favours are understood. A reader who has made a habit of the precautions the Book asks for has understood the sentence in the way it was meant. What the passage leaves with him is the timing of the matter, since the day will not offer a second appointment for those who spend this one elsewhere. Today, wealth, family standing and influential contacts can settle many earthly difficulties, which makes their complete absence from the final account especially sobering.

---

## Verse 2:124

> ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”

**ABRAHAM TESTED BY COMMANDS**

After the warning comes a figure whose story anchors much of what follows in the Book, and the sentence opens with a test: ***“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments”***. The word for testing describes a proving rather than a temptation, and the Book uses it when a person's readiness is being shown by what he does. The commands are not enumerated in the sentence, which leaves the reader to meet them in the account that follows and in the sūrah's other references to this prophet. The placement of the verse is deliberate, since the address to the Children of Israel has just closed and the sūrah now names the ancestor whose religion it claims. What the reader is given here is the beginning of an argument about who inherits the way of Abraham. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted that Abraham fulfilled the words with which he was tested, and read leadership as an honour to be followed that wrongdoing cannot inherit as a right.

**COMMANDS HE CARRIED OUT**

The test is concluded in three words, and the three words are the answer to it: ***“which he fulfilled.”***. The account of this prophet is consistently about performance rather than about position, and the verse states the fulfilment before it reports any promise. The divine speech that follows, with its promise of a role for the people, comes after the commands have been carried out, so that the order of the sentence matches the order of the story. In another passage the man is described as a model whose life matched his profession, and that is the standing verdict on him: (16:120 — **“Indeed, Abraham was a model of excellence”**). Someone given instructions who has looked for the reward before the work will find the sequence of the verse instructive.

**THE PROMISE OF A ROLE MODEL**

The sentence then reports what was said to him once the commands had been fulfilled: ***“Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model”*** and ***“for the people.”***. The term translated as a role model describes someone who is followed, and the Book's gift to Abraham is presented as an authority that others will accept rather than as a privilege he will enjoy. The promise is made in the first person, which places the appointment with the one who promises, and the same arrangement appears elsewhere in the Book. The same prophet is described in another passage as one whose way the believers are told to follow, which shows how the promise worked out in the community that came after him: (4:125 — **“follow the Way of Abraham, the upright”**). Leadership in the Book is granted to performance rather than to lineage, and the sentence says as much by the order of its clauses.

**LINEAGE STOPPED AT THE MORAL BOUNDARY**

The verse records the next exchange, which begins with a question from Abraham and a reply about a category of people: ***“Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?”*** and ***“Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”***. The question is natural for a man who had just been told that a people would follow him, and the answer directs the promise away from ancestry and toward conduct. The Book's answer does not deny the offspring anything; it denies the wrongdoers among them the covenant, which leaves the promise standing while removing the assumption behind the question. Another passage states that the prophet himself was neither of the two later communities that claimed him, which belongs to the same correction of inherited claims: (3:67 — **“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness”**). A reader who has ever rested a hope on a family connection will find the reply aimed very precisely at him.

**THE COVENANT AND THE WRONGDOERS**

That closing clause is the hinge of the sūrah's discussion of inheritance, since it states the condition on which the covenant runs. The Book uses the word for wrongdoers across the chapter for the people whose conduct and whose claims were examined, and the clause places them outside the promise rather than outside the family. The answer to Abraham's question therefore reframes the issue: what is inherited is not the bloodline but the covenant, and the covenant is not extended to those who work against its terms. Anyone who has watched a family inheritance become a source of quarrel over who qualifies will recognise the force of the correction, and the correction is made gently and in one sentence. The principle that will be applied to the communities discussed in the pages around it is what the sentence leaves behind. In the present day, leadership cannot be inherited as moral immunity, since title and lineage do not carry a wrongdoer inside a divine covenant. Leadership here is like a key entrusted after a difficult test; a descendant may inherit the family name without inheriting the key.

---

## Verse 2:125

> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺

**SANCTUARY, RETURN, AND SAFETY**

The verse continues the account of Abraham with a place rather than a promise, and it describes what was made of the sanctuary: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre”*** and ***“and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham”*** and ***“as a site of prayer.”***. The two words for the House describe a gathering point and a place of safety, and the Book treats both as gifts given to humanity rather than privileges held by one family. The instruction that follows tells the visitors what to do there, and the instruction is attached to the name of the man who built it. The sanctuary that emerges belongs to the people who come to it, with a command to use it rather than to guard it as property. Ibn ʿAbbās read the House as a place people repeatedly long to return to, its safety as protection for the entrant, and its purification as removal of idols for every form of worship named.

**THE STANDING-PLACE AND THE PRAYER SITE**

The clause about the standing-place of Abraham turns a spot associated with a man into a place of prayer for everyone who arrives, and the Book's wording makes the association a reason for the command rather than a relic to be admired. Another passage joins the same two elements when it describes the House and names the sign within it: (3:97 — **“In it are clear signs and the standing-place of Abraham”**). The verse's instruction is addressed to the visitors rather than to the man, which is worth noticing, since the sanctuary's purpose is stated in terms of what people do when they reach it. Someone who has seen a place of worship turned into a monument to its own history will find the clause's direction of attention useful, because the command is about prayer and not about veneration.

**THE TRUST TO PURIFY THE HOUSE**

The sentence then turns to the two men who were given a task: ***“And We entrusted Abraham”***, ***“and Ishmael to purify My House”***, and the task is described as purification rather than construction. The Book's word for purity here covers the removal of what does not belong in a place of worship, which is why the following clauses are about the people who use it rather than about the building's fabric. Another passage reports the same commission in the same words, and it adds the prohibition of associating anything with God in that place: (22:26 — **“purify My House for those who circle”**). The verse therefore presents the sanctuary as a trust held by two men for the benefit of everyone who comes, and the readers who inherit the story are meant to understand the work as continuing.

**A CARETAKER GIVEN THE KEYS**

Think of a caretaker handed the keys to a hall that belongs to a whole city, with instructions to keep it clean for the people who use it and not to make it his own address. The verse gives Abraham and his son exactly that kind of commission, and it names the users of the building in the clauses that follow. The comparison is useful because the temptation in such a role is always to mistake custody for ownership, and the sūrah is about to describe communities that made that mistake with an inheritance. Anyone who has seen a public building turned into a private club will understand why the next clauses describe the worshippers rather than the walls. The purpose for which the House was entrusted is what the sentence puts in front of the reader.

**CIRCLING, MEDITATING, BOWING**

The verse closes with a description of the worshippers, and the description is a list of postures: ***“for those who circle it”***, ***“who meditate in it”***, and ***“and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺”***. The three are named together without a rank among them, so that the House belongs to every kind of worshipper who comes to it. The same house is named in another passage as the starting point of a journey made at night, which shows how far the Book lets its honour travel: (17:1 — **“from the Sacred Mosque”**). The list also shows that the purification was for the sake of the people doing these things, so that the caretakers were servants of the worshippers rather than the other way around. Someone given charge of something that others use will recognise the arrangement described here, and the arrangement is the standard the Book applies to the sūrah's discussion of who may be trusted with sacred things. What remains with him is the picture of a house kept clean for the sake of those who pray in it. Today, a busy place of worship still needs physical care and moral purification so that visitors, residents and worshippers can approach without obstruction.

---

## Verse 2:126

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

**SAFETY ASKED FOR BEFORE PROVISION**

The verse records the next thing Abraham said at that place, and it is a request for two things at once: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure”*** and ***“and provide fruits to its people”***. The prayer asks for safety before it asks for provision, which places the security of the settlement ahead of its comfort, and the Book's order in the sentence is worth noticing. The request is made for a city rather than for himself, which fits the role the previous verses assigned to him as a model for others. Another passage records the same settlement being made with the same two concerns in view, and it shows how the prayer was answered in the geography of the valley: (14:37 — **“I have settled some of my offspring in a barren valley, near Your Sacred House”**). What the reader receives here is a picture of a founder who intercedes for the place he has built.

**PROVISION FOR THE PEOPLE WHO BELIEVE**

The prayer names the people for whom the provision is asked, and the clause restricts the request to those who believe: ***“those among them who believe in Allah”*** and ***“and the Last Day.”***. The Book reports the restriction because it is part of the prayer as Abraham made it, and the answer that follows will widen the provision while keeping the spiritual condition where it was. The pairing of belief in Allah with belief in the Last Day is the Book's standard way of describing a complete faith, and it appears throughout the sūrah in descriptions of the people who answer the call. The same pairing, in the note that carries Ibn ʿAbbās's name, describes the community praised earlier in this sūrah, and the verse here places the combination in the mouth of the founder. A reader should notice that the request was for provision to those who believe rather than for belief in those who are provided for.

**THE ANSWER ABOUT THOSE WHO DISBELIEVE**

The sentence then reports the divine reply, and the reply grants the prayer in a broader form while leaving the outcome of the two groups different: ***“He answered, “As”***, ***“for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves”***, ***“for a little while”*** and ***“then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”***. The provision is extended to the disbelievers for the duration of their lives, and the extension is stated as a decision rather than as an oversight. Another passage describes the same safe settlement being used as an argument by people who had not accepted the guidance: (28:57 — **“Have We not established for them a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺”**). The verse's answer therefore separates the two gifts that the prayer had joined, since security and provision were given widely while the destination was left to what each person did with his time there.

**A HOST WHO SEATS A GUEST BEFORE SHOWING HIM OUT**

Think of a host who lets a guest enjoy the meal for a while even though he knows the man will be asked to leave at the end of it. The verse's answer about the disbelievers has that shape, and the phrase about a little while keeps the whole arrangement inside a horizon that the guest cannot see. The comparison explains the absence of any condemnation in the sentence, since what is being described is a temporary provision rather than a reward. Anyone who has seen a man mistake the duration of his comfort for the quality of his position can see what the sentence is guarding against, and the guard is the clause about the destination. The difference between being provided for and being accepted is what the sentence asks him to notice.

**THE ENJOYMENT THAT IS ONLY FOR A WHILE**

The answer closes with a judgement on the place to which the disbeliever is finally sent, and the exclamation is short: what an evil destination. The Book uses such exclamations sparingly, and their appearance here marks the seriousness of the ending that follows the temporary provision. The whole reply leaves the reader with the two horizons in view at once: the food on the table and the door at the end of the meal. The fact that worldly goods are given without regard to merit fits the sūrah's argument, since provision and acceptance have been separated from the beginning. What remains after the verse is the prayer that opened it and the answer that widened it, and each person must decide which of those two horizons governs his life. Present-day prosperity reaches believers and unbelievers alike, but temporary provision does not answer the separate question of a person's final destination.

---

## Verse 2:127

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**TWO BUILDERS RAISING A FOUNDATION**

The verse returns to the building of the House and describes the work of both men, and it introduces their prayer in the same sentence: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord!”***. The verb is about laying foundations rather than finishing a structure, which places the scene at the beginning of the work, and the two men are described as praying while they build. The Book's habit of reporting the speech of its prophets in the middle of their labour gives the reader an image of work and worship as one activity. The verse follows the prayer for the city with the prayer of the builders, so that the reader moves from what was asked for the place to what was asked by the men who made it. The scene before the reader is a task carried out by two generations together. Ibn ʿAbbās placed Ishmael beside Abraham in raising the foundations and understood the closing names as knowledge of both their prayer and the intention carried in their building.

**THE PRAYER THEY MADE TOGETHER**

The words of the prayer begin with an address and move directly to a request about the work itself: ***“Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are”*** and ***“indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. The request is not for the building to stand or for the city to prosper, both of which had been asked for already, but for the work itself to be received. The two names that close the sentence are chosen for what they say about the relation between the deed and the One who sees it, since a work is heard before it is rewarded. Another passage records the same man asking for his prayers to be accepted, which shows how consistent this concern was in his life: (14:40 — **“Our Lord! Accept my prayers”**). A reader who has done something for God and wondered whether it counted has the sentence as the prayer he needs.

**ACCEPTANCE ASKED FOR AT THE START**

The Book's decision to report this request at the moment of building, rather than at the moment of finishing, is worth pausing over. The work was only beginning when the two men asked for it to be accepted, which means their concern was with the quality of what they were doing rather than with the outcome. The Book often reports the prayers of its prophets at points where the reader would expect an account of the achievement, and the effect is to place the deed inside the relationship that gives it value. A reader who has taken up a task for the sake of God will find the placement of the prayer more useful than any instruction about technique, since the request asks for the deed to be received rather than for it to succeed. What the sentence leaves with him is the practice of asking before the work is done.

**A WORKMAN ASKING THAT THE WORK BE TAKEN**

Think of a craftsman who begins a commission by asking the client to accept the piece when it is finished, before a single joint has been cut. The verse reports exactly that posture, and it names the two attributes that make the request reasonable: the One addressed hears what is asked and knows what is done. The comparison makes clear that the prayer is not a formality attached to the work but a statement about who the work is for. Anyone who has begun something difficult for the sake of God will recognise the need the prayer answers, since the doubt that troubles a person in the middle of a task has to do with acceptance rather than with ability. What the verse offers is a way to place that doubt where it belongs.

**HEARING AND KNOWING IN THEIR PRAYER**

The two names at the end of the prayer are not decorative, and the verse's choice of them explains the request they follow. A person asking for his work to be accepted needs the assurance that the request itself has been heard, and a person asking about a deed done in secret needs the assurance that it was seen. The two attributes answer both anxieties at once, and the Book places them at the close of a prayer made by men whose work would be remembered for thousands of years. Anyone who has followed the passage from the call to the Children of Israel to this scene has watched the sūrah move from a history of favours to an example of gratitude in action. What remains with him is the prayer of the two builders, and the names they used to close it. Today, builders of a mosque, school or household need the same humility: finishing the structure does not itself certify acceptance of the work.

---

## Verse 2:128

> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**SUPPLICATION RISING WITH THE WALLS**

The verse carries on the prayer that the two builders began, and it moves from their own work to the community that would come after them: ***“Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You”*** and ***“and from our descendants a nation”*** and ***“that will submit to you. Show us our rituals”***. The first request is about the two men themselves, and it asks for a state of submission rather than for a reward, which fits the posture the Book has assigned to this prophet from the beginning of his story. The second request reaches forward to a people not yet born, and it asks for the same condition in them as in their ancestors. The founder in view was concerned not with completing a building but with continuing a religion. Ibn ʿAbbās read submission as sincere obedience without association, the rites as the practices of pilgrimage, and the plea for relenting as an admission of human shortcoming.

**A NATION ASKED FOR FROM THE DESCENDANTS**

The clause about the descendants uses a word that describes a whole community rather than a family line, and the prayer asks for a nation that will submit as the two men had submitted. Another passage sums up the same history by naming the way of this prophet as a designation that God Himself gave, which shows how the request was answered: (22:78 — **“the way of your forefather Abraham”**). The hopes of the founders are placed in a people rather than in a place, and the account of the Children of Israel earlier in the sūrah has shown how often the two were confused. A community that inherits a sanctuary without inheriting the submission of its builder has inherited the smaller thing, and the prayer here asks for the greater.

**RITUALS SHOWN, NOT INVENTED**

The request about the rituals is worth a second look, since the two men ask to be shown rather than to be left to work the matter out. The Book's treatment of worship in this sūrah is consistently about what has been prescribed rather than what has been devised, and the prayer states the principle in three words. Another passage describes the community that resulted by listing what the messenger did among them, and the list begins with recitation and purification before it reaches the teaching of the Book: (2:151 — **“reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you”**). The order in the prayer is therefore the order the Book keeps elsewhere, with the showing and the following placed before everything else.

**TWO REQUESTS IN ONE BREATH**

The verse then asks for a turning in grace, and it closes with the two names that make the request reasonable: ***“and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. The men who were building a house of worship asked to be received, and the Book records the request in the same breath as their work. The names used at the end are the ones a person needs when he has built and cannot assess what he has built: one who accepts the return, and one whose mercy is not exhausted. The reader has already heard the same man asking for his prayers to be accepted, and the repetition shows how the posture of the builder and the posture of the supplicant were one thing in this prophet. Another passage names the same attribute for a community in distress, which shows how the Book uses it when a person has nothing left but the request: (9:118 — **“And ˹Allah has also turned in mercy to˺ the three who had remained behind”**). What the sentence leaves with him is the practice of ending work with a request for pardon.

**BUILDERS STILL IN NEED OF INSTRUCTION**

Think of a man who finishes a wall for a mosque and then asks the owner of the land to forgive him for the parts he did poorly. The verse does not separate the work from the request, and the two are placed together in the same prayer. The comparison matters because the Book's account of worship treats confidence and humility as partners rather than alternatives, and the men in the scene had both in full measure. Anyone who has completed something for God and then examined it honestly will know why the sentence asks for grace after asking for guidance. The acceptance of a community begins with the acknowledgment that it has nothing to present on its own account, which is why the request for grace stands beside the work. In the present day, inherited religious identity remains incomplete until practice is learned, shortcomings are admitted and submission is deliberately renewed. It follows that even Abraham's household did not treat submission as self-sustaining, because guidance, ritual knowledge and repentance are all requested together.

---

## Verse 2:129

> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**A MESSENGER ASKED FOR FROM WITHIN THE NATION**

The prayer reaches its highest request in this verse, and the thing asked for is a person rather than a building, since the descendants will need someone to teach them what their ancestor could only ask for on their behalf: ***“Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger”*** and ***“who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book”***. The prophet who is praying asks for a prophet to come after him from among his own descendants, which is a remarkable thing for a founder to request. The Book reports the request without comment, and the answer to it shaped the history that the sūrah has been addressing. The line of Abraham was expected to produce something more than a nation with a sanctuary, and the prayer says so by asking for a messenger. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the requested messenger as one from Ishmael's descendants, wisdom as instruction in the lawful and prohibited, and purification as release from sin through divine oneness.

**FOUR TASKS IN AN ORDER**

The verse lists four tasks and they are given in an order: recitation, teaching of the Book, wisdom, and purification. The order moves from what is heard to what is understood to what is lived, the sequence the Book follows whenever it describes guidance taking hold of a community. Another passage describes the same sending in nearly the same words and calls it a favour done to the believers, which places the answer to this prayer among the gifts named in the sūrah: (62:2 — **“He is the One Who raised for the illiterate ˹people˺ a messenger from among themselves”**). The messenger is not asked for as a ruler or a conqueror but as a teacher, and the community that receives him is described by what it is taught.

**THE PURIFICATION THAT COMES LAST AND FIRST**

Purification is named at the end of the list, and the Book places it after the teaching rather than before it. The order suggests that the community is purified by what it learns rather than prepared for learning by being purified, which is the pattern the sūrah follows in its description of the believers. Another passage lists the same activities in a different order and puts purification before the teaching of wisdom, which shows that the sequence is not rigid: (2:151 — **“reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you”**). The four tasks together describe a transformation that runs through the ear, the mind and the conduct, and the prayer asks for all of them at once because none of them is sufficient alone.

**A GARDENER WHO ASKS FOR THE WATERING**

Think of a man who plants a tree and then asks that someone be sent to water it, knowing that his own lifetime will not cover the tree's growth. The prayer in this verse has that shape, since it asks for a messenger who will do among the descendants what the founder could not do himself. The request is made by a prophet rather than by an ordinary man, since only someone who knows the size of the task would ask for it in these terms. Anyone who has started something that will outlast him will understand the logic of the sentence, and the logic is that the work needs a person, not a plan. The shape of the answer that history gave to the prayer is what the verse sets before him.

**POWER AND WISDOM AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with an address to God under two names, and the names describe power and wisdom rather than mercy: ***“and wisdom, and purify them.”*** and ***“Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”***. The choice is fitted to the request, since the raising of a messenger requires an authority that nothing can resist and a wisdom that places him in the right nation at the right time. The Book frequently closes a request with the names that answer it, and the practice is visible here in a single sentence. A reader who has traced the prayer from its beginning will notice that the whole sequence has been about submission, ritual, grace and teaching, and the verse ends by naming the two attributes that make all of it possible. What remains when the prayer closes is the account of how the community that inherited it behaved. The prayer's own two names answer the request it makes, and the account of the covenant and the calf has already shown what happens when a community inherits a message without the teaching that belongs with it. Another passage calls the answer to this prayer a favour done to the believers, which places the messenger's work among the gifts the sūrah has been counting: (3:164 — **“Indeed, Allah has done the believers a ˹great˺ favour”**). Today, communities need more than information: they need truthful recitation, sound judgement and the purification of habits that knowledge alone may leave intact.

---

## Verse 2:130

> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous

**THE FOOL IN THE QUESTION**

The people who might turn away from what Abraham had are addressed next, and the question asked about them leaves no room for a respectable reply: ***“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool!”***. The Book's word for the fool describes a person whose judgement has failed him rather than one who lacks information, and the exclamation marks the verdict as settled. The sūrah has just recorded the prayer of the founder, and the sentence now asks what kind of person would turn away from the way the founder prayed for. The question is addressed to the reader as much as to the communities around him, since the objection it anticipates could belong to anyone. The rejection of this way is a failure of understanding rather than a difference of taste, which is what the question assumes. Ibn ʿAbbās read rejection of Abraham's way as self-ruin and folly, while the choice in this world included prophethood, submission and a sound line of descendants.

**A MAN SELECTED IN THIS LIFE**

The sentence then states the position of the man whose faith is under discussion, and the word chosen for it recurs in the sūrah's treatment of the prophets: ***“We certainly chose him in this life”***. The choice belongs explicitly to this world, which places the honour before any mention of the reward that follows it. The Book uses the language of selection for prophets and for communities, and the same verb appears in the verses about the choice of the believers which the sūrah has already discussed. Another passage describes the man as one who followed the guidance of his Lord and was described as upright, which is the Book's fuller account of the choosing: (6:161 — **“the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists”**). The reader is being shown what the choosing looked like in a life rather than in a title.

**SELF-RUIN THROUGH REJECTING ABRAHAM**

The verse also has a practical function in the argument of the sūrah, since it turns the question of who belongs to Abraham into a question about what Abraham did. The communities that claimed him had made him one of their own, and the sentence identifies the content of his way as something separate from their claims: he was chosen, and his choosing is the standard against which the claims are measured. Another passage puts the matter in the form of a comparison and asks who could be better in faith than those who follow this way, which is the positive form of the question asked here: (4:125 — **“And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah”**). The argument narrows here to a single test, which the sūrah's treatment of inheritance has been preparing.

**A SHOP THAT TURNS AWAY ITS BEST CUSTOMERS**

Think of a shop that refuses to serve the customers its own founder taught it to expect, and that then complains that its shelves are full. The verse asks what to call a person who turns away from a way that was laid down by the man he claims as a father, and the word chosen for him is not a polite one. The comparison shows how the Book treats the rejection of guidance when the guidance has a clear history: the failure is one of judgement rather than of evidence, and the sentence says so in a question. Anyone who has watched a community inherit a tradition and keep only its name can see what the question is pointing at. The plain sense left behind is that a great inheritance can be refused by a person who thinks himself wise.

**WHERE THE CHOSEN MAN ENDED UP**

The outcome of that choosing in the next life is named at the close: ***“and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”***. The sentence connects the honor of this world to a standing in the next, which is the Book's pattern when it describes the people it approves. The word for the righteous is the same word used of the conduct that the sūrah has been demanding from the communities that received scriptures, and it places this prophet among those whose record is sound. The choosing stated earlier in the verse therefore ends where the Book says such choices end, which is why the sentence gives the man a standing in both worlds. The Book's argument about inheritance therefore ends with a statement of where the ancestor himself ended up, which leaves the claims of his descendants to be judged against it. The picture left is of a man whose faith, choice and destination are described in three clauses. Present-day appeals to Abraham are tested by whether they preserve his submission or use his name to defend the very pride he abandoned. The effect of calling rejection self-folly is to move the loss inside the rejecter, since Abraham's chosen standing cannot be diminished by another person's refusal.

---

## Verse 2:131

> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**THE REPLY THAT NEEDED NO PAUSE**

This verse is the shortest exchange in the whole account, and it records a command and its acceptance in a single sentence: ***“When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.””***. The Book reports no deliberation between the two halves, and the absence of a pause is the point of the sentence. The command is given in the same form the prayer of the previous verses used, and the answer returns the word to its giver in a longer and more specific phrase. The verse therefore shows the submission that Abraham had asked for on behalf of himself and his descendants being performed in his own case first. Anyone who has asked God for a quality and then been tested in it will recognise the sequence. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted readings that place Abraham's answer after the fire and during his call to his people, but all converge on sincerity of religion and works to the Lord of every realm.

**NO PAUSE BETWEEN THE TWO HALVES**

The Book's prophets are shown receiving instructions in different ways, and this one is given as a direct address with no accompanying explanation. The sentence does not record what the man understood the submission to involve, and it does not record him asking either. Another passage places the same prophet in a scene where he is asked to explain his faith, and his answer there is a statement of what he was guided to rather than a defence: (6:161 — **“the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists”**). The brevity of this verse is a statement about the man as much as about the command, since the Book's account of him turns on the speed of his compliance.

**WHO THE ANSWER NAMES**

The response is worth reading closely because it names the One obeyed rather than the command received: he submits to the Lord of all worlds. The phrase is a declaration about the reach of the authority being accepted, and it answers the command by stating the scope of what is being handed over. The Book has already used the same title in the sūrah's opening verses, where the Lord of all worlds is named as the one who sent down the Book, so the reader meets a phrase here that the chapter has taught him from its start. A submission made to a local or tribal deity would have been a smaller thing; the phrase chosen by the man makes his acceptance universal, and the Book records the choice of words without comment. The argument about the religion of Abraham reaches its plainest statement in the man's own mouth.

**A SERVANT WHO ANSWERS THE CALL BY NAME**

Think of a craftsman who is asked to hand over his workshop and who replies by naming the owner of the city rather than the man who spoke to him. The answer in the verse has that quality, since it bypasses the command and addresses the commander, and the acceptance is complete because the person is. The comparison also shows why the Book treats this exchange as a definition of the faith it is discussing: submission is not the performance of one instruction but the handing over of oneself to the one who gives it. Anyone who has tried to obey in a piecemeal way will find the sentence's brevity instructive, since the answer given here is about a Lord and not about a task. The shape of a whole acceptance is what the sentence offers.

**THE PLACEMENT OF THE EXCHANGE**

The sūrah records the exchange between the prayer for a community and the advice the man later gave his children, and its position is part of its meaning. The verse shows the ancestor doing what he had asked God to make him and his descendants do, which closes the circle opened by the earlier request. The Book follows the same method in other places, where a prophet's prayer is answered by a scene in which the prophet himself acts out what he asked for. The prayer for a submitting nation and the founder's own submission in one sentence together give the whole account: what is at stake is a handover rather than a heritage. What remains when the sentence ends is the example it set for the family that came after. Today, a decisive act of surrender can be stated in a moment yet must govern the work, loyalties and fears that follow it.

---

## Verse 2:132

> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**AN ANCESTOR'S ADVICE TO HIS CHILDREN**

The verse reports what the man said to his own household, and it names two generations in the same sentence: ***“This was the advice of Abraham”***, ***“as well as Jacob”***, ***“to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen”***. The advice is not recorded as a private conviction but as something handed on to children, which places the instruction inside the family at the moment the family was becoming a nation. Jacob is named beside Abraham, which extends the same counsel across another lifetime and shows that the tradition had a lineage rather than a single author. The religion of Abraham has been described in this sūrah by what he did and what he was promised, and this verse adds the act of transmission. The inheritance here is deliberately given rather than passively received. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the dying instruction of Abraham and Jacob as a charge to hold fast to divine oneness until death, not merely to inherit a communal name.

**WHAT WAS CHOSEN FOR THEM**

The advice opens with a statement about what God did rather than about what the family had: ***“for you this faith”*** and ***“so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”***. The faith is described as chosen for the children, which places the initiative with God and the response with the people who receive it. The instruction that follows is about dying in a state rather than about performing a single act, and the wording makes the state the goal of a whole life.
