When a created love agrees with obedience to Allah, it becomes a blessing. When it makes a person reject Allah, violate rights, or sacrifice truth, it has become a rival. The believers’ love for God is stronger and undivided. Their love is not a momentary emotion. It is rooted in recognizing Allah’s perfection, mercy, lordship, and countless gifts. It appears in obedience when desire pulls in another direction, in gratitude during ease, patience during hardship, repentance after sin, and preference for truth over applause. Love of Allah produces both intimacy and awe. The believer hopes in mercy, fears displeasing Him, longs to meet Him, and trusts His wisdom. The Qur’an describes love as a mark of faith and says that those who believe are more intense in love for Allah because no rival divides the centre of their devotion. (2:163 — **“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”**) Because rivals in love and worship governs 2:165, the test of competing loves arises from rivals in love and worship. It follows that love and justice completes rivals in love and worship through the test of competing loves.

**THE TEST OF COMPETING LOVES**

***“but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more.”***, ***“If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize”***, ***“that all power belongs to Allah”*** establish the test of competing loves. A person can examine his hierarchy of love through choices. Conflicts between truth and reputation disclose what a person protects; conflicts between lawful income and profit disclose what he obeys; and choices about clothing, speech, friendship, and public conduct disclose whose approval governs him. The answers reveal whether Allah is loved above all or merely included among other priorities. The Prophet ﷺ said that none truly believes until he loves the Messenger more than his parent, child, and all people, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; another authentic hadith describes the sweetness of faith when Allah and His Messenger are more beloved than everything else. This does not make the Prophet an object of worship. It means loving him as Allah’s messenger and following him because of Allah. The verse suddenly turns toward the Day of Punishment: If only the wrongdoers could see. Their false hierarchy will then be exposed. They will see that all power—all power—belongs to Allah, while the rivals they obeyed possess no independent control. The phrase is a picture of regret: the truth becomes undeniable only after the opportunity to act upon it has ended. In this world, power may appear to belong to rulers, armies, money, or public opinion. These are created means, and Allah may allow them influence for a time. But no means operates outside His knowledge and permission. On the Day of Resurrection, the illusion of independent power disappears, and every false allegiance is seen in its true weakness. (9:24 — **“˹if all these˺ are more beloved to you than Allah”**) The reason love and justice follows the test of competing loves lies in rivals in love and worship. Therefore, love and justice returns practical force to the test of competing loves.

**LOVE AND JUSTICE**

For love and justice, the decisive wording is ***“and that Allah is”***, ***“indeed severe in punishment”***. The verse links shirk with wrongdoing—*al-ẓulm*. Giving worship to other than Allah is the greatest injustice because it places a created thing in the position of the Creator. It also creates secondary injustices: people may obey idols of tribe, race, nation, or leader and then oppress others to protect them. Pure love of Allah, by contrast, disciplines power. The servant knows that he will answer for how he treats people and creation. He can love his family deeply without owning them, love his homeland without worshipping nationalism, and respect a leader without obeying him in sin. Love grows through knowing Allah’s names, reciting and reflecting upon the Qur’an, remembering blessings, performing obligatory worship, engaging in voluntary deeds, and observing the effects of obedience on the heart. The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah’s servant draws near through obligations and then through voluntary works until Allah loves him, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. Love also grows when a believer notices Allah’s mercy in forgiveness and guidance. It is not built only through fear. The names *al-Raḥmān* and *the Most Merciful* in the preceding verse show that the One who deserves ultimate love is the One whose mercy surrounds His servants. Picture a passenger who thanks the dashboard for a safe journey while ignoring the driver, because the glowing instruments are what he can see and touch. The instruments may be useful, but they neither chose the road nor preserved the traveller. Rivals set beside God occupy the dashboard's place: created means are treated as sources, and dependence is mistaken for worship. In a present-day culture of brands, leaders, and systems, love must pass through created means without stopping at them. (31:13 — **“while advising him, “O my dear son!”**) In other words, love and justice answers rivals in love and worship.

---

## Verse 2:166

> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off

**THE COLLAPSE OF FALSE LEADERSHIP**

The wording for the collapse of false leadership is ***“˹Consider the Day˺ when those”***, ***“who misled others will disown their followers”***. The verse describes a scene from the Hereafter in which followers and leaders discover that their worldly relationship cannot save them. Those who were followed—rulers, religious figures, celebrities, ancestors, ideologues, or charismatic personalities—disown those who followed them. The followers had treated created beings as authorities deserving unquestioning loyalty, but the leaders had no power to carry their burdens before Allah. The verse does not condemn every form of following. Muslims follow prophets, qualified scholars, parents in what is right, and legitimate authority within the limits of Allah’s law. The condemned following is blind allegiance that continues in falsehood after evidence has arrived, or obedience to a person in disobedience to Allah. The leaders’ disavowal is not necessarily evidence that every leader was innocent. Some were themselves deceivers who encouraged the following for status or gain. Others may have been worshipped or obeyed beyond what they claimed. The scene reveals that the relationship was based on mutual illusion: followers expected rescue from leaders, and leaders enjoyed influence without accepting responsibility for the consequences. The Qur’an elsewhere records Iblīs saying that he had no authority except that he called and people responded. His statement does not absolve him from deception, but it exposes the followers’ responsibility to choose. No created being can force the heart to worship. Both the deceiver and the willing follower face the consequences of their own choices. (2:165 — **“Still there are some”**) Because the collapse of false leadership governs 2:166, when punishment is seen arises from the collapse of false leadership. It follows that the responsibility of followers completes the collapse of false leadership through when punishment is seen.

**WHEN PUNISHMENT IS SEEN**

The movement toward when punishment is seen rests on ***“when they face the torment”***. In the Hereafter, the reality is visible. The followers see that the power they feared was temporary, the leader they praised was helpless, and the obedience they offered did not produce salvation. The Qur’an repeatedly describes this moment so that people can break false allegiances before death. A servant should ask now whether his loyalty is based on truth or on the fear of losing a group. The ability to change one’s allegiance is a mercy available in the world; in the Hereafter, regret cannot create a new test. All ties between them are cut off refers to the causes of relationship that once united them—*asbāb*. It may include claims of kinship, political alliances, shared ideology, promises of intercession, and mutual support in wrongdoing. The Qur’an does not mean that every family relationship ceases to have any emotional memory; it means that no worldly tie can function as a means of rescue when it was not established upon faith and righteousness. This is not a reason to neglect family or community. Islam commands maintaining kinship and honouring lawful commitments. It is a warning against assuming that blood, nationality, membership, or proximity to a famous person automatically transfers spiritual benefit. The useful relationship is one that encourages truth and obedience. (14:21 — **“so will you ˹then˺ protect us from Allah’s torment in any way?””**) The reason the responsibility of followers follows when punishment is seen lies in the collapse of false leadership. Therefore, the responsibility of followers returns practical force to when punishment is seen.

**THE RESPONSIBILITY OF FOLLOWERS**

The sequence reaches the responsibility of followers through ***“and the bonds that united them will be cut off”***. Followers often say, I was only obeying my leader, but the Qur’an rejects this as a complete excuse. The Prophet ﷺ taught that there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator. A person must use discernment, ask for evidence, and refuse commands that clearly violate Allah’s law. Respect for elders or scholars does not mean treating them as infallible. This responsibility is especially important in movements that demand absolute loyalty, silence criticism, or portray outsiders as less than human. A Muslim may cooperate in good but must retain conscience, justice, and accountability before Allah. No group identity can cancel individual responsibility. Those who lead others carry an even heavier trust. The Prophet ﷺ said that every person is a shepherd and every person is responsible for his flock, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. A leader cannot wait until the Hereafter to claim that followers misunderstood him if he knowingly encouraged falsehood or exploited their devotion. Religious leaders should teach divine oneness rather than make themselves indispensable. Political and community leaders should welcome accountability rather than demand worshipful obedience. The best leadership directs people to Allah; the worst leadership makes itself the centre of their fear and hope. A crowd may follow a guide through a dangerous building, only to discover at the locked exit that he never possessed a key. At that moment admiration turns into accusation, but mutual blame does not open the door. The scene of disowned followers is like that failed evacuation: borrowed confidence collapses when responsibility arrives. Anyone choosing a teacher, movement, or admired voice today should therefore ask before the crisis whether the path is true, rather than hoping loyalty itself will become an excuse. (28:63 — **“Those ˹misleaders˺ against whom the decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will cry, “Our Lord!”**) In other words, the responsibility of followers answers the collapse of false leadership.

---

## Verse 2:167

> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire

**REGRET WITHOUT A SECOND TRIAL**

At regret without a second trial, attention falls on ***“The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them”***, ***“as they disowned us.””***. The followers respond to the leaders’ disavowal with a wish for another opportunity: If only we had another chance. They now recognize that the leaders could not help them and that their obedience was misplaced. They promise to reject those leaders just as the leaders have rejected them. But the wish comes after the test has ended. The Qur’an repeatedly presents such regret to teach the living. Regret is useful when it leads to repentance and change, but regret after death cannot create new deeds. A wise person listens to the warning before the consequences are visible. He examines the people he follows, the assumptions he inherits, and the desires that govern his decisions while correction remains possible. The followers’ words imply an admission of responsibility. They do not simply say, *Our leaders ruined us*; they say that if returned, they would disown them. This shows that they know they participated in the alliance. They chose to follow, defended the leaders, and perhaps benefited from the false system. A person cannot surrender his moral judgement to another and then expect to be free of accountability. This does not deny that leaders can manipulate, threaten, or deceive. Allah judges coercion, knowledge, capacity, and influence perfectly. But ordinary claims of *I was only following orders* do not excuse a person who could recognize and refuse wrongdoing. The Qur’an asks people to use hearing, sight, and reason rather than surrendering their conscience. (2:166 — **“˹Consider the Day˺ when those”**) Because regret without a second trial governs 2:167, deeds become sources of regret arises from regret without a second trial. It follows that returning to the present completes regret without a second trial through deeds become sources of regret.

**DEEDS BECOME SOURCES OF REGRET**

Deeds become sources of regret draws together ***“And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds.”***. Allah will show them their deeds as regrets. The phrase suggests that the very actions in which they once found pride, pleasure, or belonging will become objects of pain. Wealth gained through injustice, loyalty offered to falsehood, time wasted in mockery, and opportunities for good deliberately abandoned will all appear in their true form. The Qur’an says that a person will see what he sent ahead. Deeds are not erased by death or hidden behind public reputation. When the curtain lifts, the person sees how every choice shaped his final state. They will never leave the Fire describes the final punishment of those who die upon disbelief and persist in the allegiance to falsehood described in the passage. The permanence is not a denial of Allah’s mercy; it is the consequence of meeting Allah in a state that rejects Him. Muslims affirm the warning while entrusting the detailed judgement of individuals to Allah’s perfect knowledge and justice. The verse should produce seriousness about the Hereafter, not a culture of cruelty. The Prophet ﷺ grieved over people’s rejection and sought ways to guide them. Believers warn because they want people saved, and they invite through wisdom, mercy, and clear evidence rather than celebrating another person’s destruction. (67:10 — **“And they will lament, “If only we had listened”**) The reason returning to the present follows deeds become sources of regret lies in regret without a second trial. Therefore, returning to the present returns practical force to deeds become sources of regret.

**RETURNING TO THE PRESENT**

***“And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire”*** mark the turn toward returning to the present. The phrase if only we had another chance should be transformed into action now. A person who recognizes a harmful influence can leave it. Someone who followed a false opinion can seek sound knowledge. A community that has defended injustice can acknowledge it, repair the harm, and change its structures. Repentance is not merely feeling ashamed; it is breaking the alliance with falsehood before it becomes permanent. The believer should also remember that influence is reciprocal. A follower can strengthen a leader by praise, money, votes, silence, or repeated sharing of harmful speech. Refusing to participate in falsehood is a form of worship. Supporting a good leader is likewise a good deed when the support remains within truth and accountability. Imagine watching a recording of a bridge collapse and seeing the warning signs that were ignored before the fall. The viewer aches to enter the scene, stop the traffic, and redirect every car, but the recording cannot be reopened and the consequences cannot be revised. The regret described here has that closed quality. A person living this week still possesses what the people in the scene seek—time in which attachment can be tested, harmful loyalty broken, and a different road taken before deeds become only memories. (33:66 — **“If only we had obeyed Allah”**) In other words, returning to the present answers regret without a second trial.

---

## Verse 2:168

> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy

**A UNIVERSAL INVITATION**

***“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”*** establish a universal invitation. After describing false allegiance and the regret of those who followed leaders in error, Allah addresses all humanity. The command to eat *lawful and wholesome*—what is lawful and wholesome—shows that Islam’s guidance concerns ordinary life as well as formal worship. Food sustains the body, shapes habits, affects family life and commerce, and becomes part of the servant’s relationship with Allah. The address is universal, not limited to Muslims. Allah’s provision is made available to humanity, and everyone is called to recognize its lawful limits and its moral source. For believers, the command is also a test of gratitude: they do not consume whatever desire or market power can obtain, but ask whether it is lawful, wholesome, and acquired without injustice. *Lawful* means permitted by the divine law, while *wholesome* includes what is wholesome, clean, beneficial, and suitable. The two terms are related but not identical. Food may be technically permissible in its ingredients yet harmful through contamination, abuse, or an unlawful method of acquisition. Wealth may purchase a lawful product while the money used to buy it came from theft, fraud, bribery, or exploitation. The command therefore includes the source, substance, preparation, and effect of consumption. Muslims examine labels and ingredients where needed, avoid intoxicants and harmful substances, and seek trustworthy information without falling into obsessive doubt. They also remember that lawful food does not excuse waste. The Qur’an commands eating and drinking without extravagance. (5:87 — **“O believers! Do not forbid the good things”**) Because a universal invitation governs 2:168, the enemy’s incremental path arises from a universal invitation. It follows that consumption and spiritual health completes a universal invitation through the enemy’s incremental path.

**THE ENEMY’S INCREMENTAL PATH**

For the enemy’s incremental path, the decisive wording is ***“and good on the earth”***. Allah does not merely say, *Do not follow Satan*; He says, *Do not follow his footsteps*—Satan’s footsteps. Evil often develops gradually. A person begins with a doubtful transaction, normalizes a small deception, accepts a gift that influences his judgement, and eventually consumes wealth or food known to be forbidden. Satan invites through incremental steps so that the destination is hidden behind ordinary choices. The same pattern appears in speech, dress, relationships, and ideology. The believer watches the path, not only the final act. He avoids environments and habits that repeatedly pull him toward sin, and he seeks lawful alternatives before temptation becomes dominant. Satan’s enmity is clear because he seeks to corrupt the human relationship with Allah. He wants people to treat blessings as independent possessions, to consume without gratitude, and to define right and wrong according to desire. His promises are decorated with convenience and freedom, but they end in enslavement to appetite, debt, addiction, and regret. The Qur’an says Satan commands obscenity and false speech about Allah. The next verse explains how food restrictions and religious claims can be manipulated. People may declare lawful what Allah forbade or forbid what Allah allowed, then attribute their preferences to revelation. This is one of Satan’s most dangerous steps: turning desire into theology. (7:31 — **“Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat”**) The reason consumption and spiritual health follows the enemy’s incremental path lies in a universal invitation. Therefore, consumption and spiritual health returns practical force to the enemy’s incremental path.

**CONSUMPTION AND SPIRITUAL HEALTH**

Read under consumption and spiritual health, the relevant clauses are ***“and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy”***. The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah is good and accepts only what is good, then mentioned the person who travels, raises his hands in supplication, while his food, drink, clothing, and nourishment are unlawful, leaving the conditions of a sound response gravely impaired. This hadith, recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, connects lawful consumption with the health of worship. Allah answers supplication in His wisdom. It is a warning that unlawful income and consumption can place barriers before spiritual life. A believer who wants a responsive heart should care about contracts, wages, ingredients, and the rights of producers and workers. Food is a gift from Allah, even when it reaches the table through human labour. Gratitude includes saying Allah’s name, avoiding waste, sharing with others, and recognizing the people and land involved in production. The Prophet ﷺ taught moderation and encouraged sharing food. The Qur’an condemns those who hoard or consume wealth unjustly. A community guided by this verse supports food security, honest trade, humane treatment of animals, and access to nutritious food for the poor. Individual piety cannot be separated from the economic conditions that determine whether people can obtain wholesome provision. Food law here is like a clear path through an orchard whose owner has opened abundant fruit but marked a few dangerous plots. Wisdom neither starves at the gate nor tears down every marker; it receives the permitted abundance and respects the boundaries. The footsteps of Satan begin when appetite persuades a person that the marked route is needless or that invented fences are holier than the owner's directions. Present-day consumption still tests both errors: careless indulgence and religious restrictions God never imposed. (16:114 — **“So eat from the good, lawful things”**) In other words, consumption and spiritual health answers a universal invitation.

---

## Verse 2:169

> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know

**SATAN’S TWO GREAT INVITATIONS**

The movement toward satan’s two great invitations rests on ***“He only incites you to commit evil”***. This verse explains Satan’s footsteps. He commands evil in general, and *indecency*, obscene or gross immorality. He also commands people to say about Allah what they do not know. The first corrupts conduct; the second corrupts belief and law. Together they destroy both the servant’s relationship with Allah and his relationships with people. Satan’s command is an invitation, not a power that compels. He whispers, beautifies, exaggerates, and presents sin as freedom, but he cannot force the person who seeks refuge in Allah and uses his will responsibly. On the Day of Resurrection, Satan will say that he had no authority except that he called and people responded. *Evil* includes disbelief, injustice, betrayal, cruelty, and every action that Allah dislikes. *Indecency* is more specific to shameless and indecent acts, especially those that violate sexual morality, family dignity, or the natural sense of modesty. The Qur’an does not treat immorality as a private matter without social consequences. It harms individuals, families, and communities, and it normalizes the humiliation or exploitation of the vulnerable. The believer protects himself through modesty, lawful relationships, lowered gaze, truthful companionship, and distance from media or environments that repeatedly make indecency attractive. He also avoids becoming self-righteous. Allah commands opposition to sin with wisdom and justice, not with slander, spying, or cruelty. (2:168 — **“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”**) Because satan’s two great invitations governs 2:169, speaking about allah without knowledge arises from satan’s two great invitations. It follows that desire disguised as religion completes satan’s two great invitations through speaking about allah without knowledge.

**SPEAKING ABOUT ALLAH WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE**

The sequence reaches speaking about allah without knowledge through ***“and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know”***. Ibn ʿAbbās included every act of disobedience within the evil named here. The second command is especially dangerous: inventing claims about Allah without knowledge. This includes declaring something lawful or unlawful without evidence, attributing a false statement to revelation, explaining the Qur’an from personal whim, denying a divine attribute without understanding, or issuing confident religious rulings beyond one’s competence. The Qur’an places saying about Allah what you do not know among the gravest prohibitions. A person may be physically abstinent while spiritually violating this command through misinformation. False theology can lead people into worship of other than Allah, unjust treatment of others, or despair of divine mercy. The opposite of speaking without knowledge is intellectual humility. The Prophet ﷺ answered questions directly when revelation had clarified them and waited for revelation when it had not. His Companions and the classical scholars frequently said, *Allah knows best,* not as a performance of modesty but as recognition of responsibility. A student should verify a hadith before sharing it, distinguish a scholar’s opinion from an explicit verse, and avoid presenting a disputed matter as unanimous. Social media makes the sin easier because a short statement can reach thousands before it is corrected. The believer slows down when the subject is Allah, His Book, and the rights of people. (7:33 — **“a practice He has never authorized”**) The reason desire disguised as religion follows speaking about allah without knowledge lies in satan’s two great invitations. Therefore, desire disguised as religion returns practical force to speaking about allah without knowledge.

**DESIRE DISGUISED AS RELIGION**

Satan may lead a person first through appetite and then through justification. Someone wants a forbidden profit, a relationship, or a ritual innovation, so he searches for a religious sentence that will approve it. Alternatively, someone dislikes a command and declares it irrational or obsolete without studying its evidence. In both cases, desire has become the hidden author of theology. The cure is to return to the Qur’an, authentic Sunnah, Arabic meanings, the understanding of the Companions, and qualified scholarship. A believer does not treat every inherited custom as revelation or every personal preference as a principle of Islam. Satan’s clear enmity does not mean that a believer is helpless. The Qur’an teaches seeking refuge in Allah, reciting the last two chapters, maintaining remembrance, and filling the heart with beneficial knowledge and good action. When a whisper appears, the servant does not debate it endlessly; he seeks refuge, abandons the path, and turns to a lawful alternative. Repentance also breaks Satan’s strategy. If a person falls, he should not conclude that he is permanently corrupt. Allah loves those who repent and purify themselves. The enemy wants both the sin and the despair that follows it; sincere *tawbah* denies him both victories. False teaching often works like a forged label placed on a harmful medicine. The substance is already dangerous, but the false label adds a second injury by claiming the authority of the healer. Evil and indecency harm conduct; speaking about God without knowledge then recruits religion to protect the harm. In today's rapid streams of clips, posts, and confident answers, the verse requires a pause before forwarding a ruling: certainty of tone is not evidence, and sacred language does not turn invention into truth. (16:116 — **“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful”**) In other words, desire disguised as religion answers satan’s two great invitations.

---

## Verse 2:170

> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance

**INHERITED PRACTICE AND REVEALED GUIDANCE**

Inherited practice and revealed guidance draws together ***“When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No!”***. The verse describes people who answer a call to follow revelation with an appeal to ancestral custom. They do not say, We examined the evidence and found it unconvincing. They say, We will follow what we found our forefathers doing. Their argument is social rather than intellectual: the practice is old, familiar, and attached to respected names, so it must be preserved. Islam honours righteous ancestors, family ties, and beneficial tradition. The problem is not that a practice has been inherited. Much of religious knowledge is transmitted through trustworthy teachers and communities. The problem is treating ancestry as a proof that can overrule Allah’s revelation. A custom is evaluated by truth; truth is not evaluated merely by age. The rhetorical question exposes the weakness of blind imitation. The rebuke assumes that ancestors may have lacked understanding, investigation, and guidance. Reverence for parents cannot require following them into shirk or injustice. The Qur’an commands kindness to parents while stating that they must not be obeyed in associating partners with Allah. Good family relations and independent moral responsibility coexist. The verse is not an insult to every forefather. Some ancestors were knowledgeable and guided, and following their sound teaching can be praiseworthy. It is directed at people who use ancestry as a shield against clear evidence, even when the inherited practice is demonstrably false or harmful. (2:168 — **“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”**) Because inherited practice and revealed guidance governs 2:170, blind imitation and responsible learning arises from inherited practice and revealed guidance. It follows that the courage to break a harmful pattern completes inherited practice and revealed guidance through blind imitation and responsible learning.

**BLIND IMITATION AND RESPONSIBLE LEARNING**

***“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even”*** mark the turn toward taqlīd and responsible learning. The Arabic concept of *blind imitation* can mean following a qualified authority without personally deriving every ruling from its evidence. For a non-specialist, asking scholars is necessary and reasonable: Ask the people of knowledge if you do not know. The condemned imitation is not all reliance on scholarship; it is stubborn adherence to an inherited position after the truth has become clear, or following an unqualified person simply because he is famous or familiar. Responsible learning combines trust with discernment. The ordinary believer consults reliable scholars, compares claims with the Qur’an and authentic Sunnah, and avoids making every personal preference into an independent legal school. The scholar, in turn, does not demand loyalty to himself in place of loyalty to Allah. Every society has customs that appear natural because they are repeated. Some are harmless or beneficial; others preserve discrimination, exploitation, superstition, or family abuse. The verse asks Muslims to examine inherited practices through the principles of revelation. A tradition that strengthens honesty, hospitality, kinship, and justice may be retained. A tradition that violates divine oneness or human rights must be corrected, even if correction is unpopular. The same warning applies to modern customs. People sometimes reject revelation while claiming to follow *what everyone does.* Modernity is not automatically guidance, just as antiquity is not automatically truth. The Qur’an gives a criterion independent of fashion and ancestry. (5:104 — **“if their forefathers had absolutely no knowledge or guidance”**) The reason the courage to break a harmful pattern follows blind imitation and responsible learning lies in inherited practice and revealed guidance. Therefore, the courage to break a harmful pattern returns practical force to blind imitation and responsible learning.

**THE COURAGE TO BREAK A HARMFUL PATTERN**

The verse develops the courage to break a harmful pattern with ***“if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance”***. Following revelation can require a person to disappoint relatives or leave a familiar environment. This must be done with wisdom, patience, and good character. The believer does not humiliate parents or insult a culture when rejecting a false practice. He explains the reason, preserves lawful ties, and refuses obedience only where obedience would violate Allah’s command. Prophets repeatedly stood against the inherited religion of their people. Ibrāhīm confronted the worship of idols while speaking with clarity and courage. His example shows that loyalty to truth is not disrespect for family; it is the highest form of concern when a family is travelling toward harm. An inherited route can be like a trail worn deep across a field: its depth proves that many feet used it, not that it reaches the right destination. A traveller still needs a map and must be willing to leave the track when it leads away from safety. Family custom and communal habit have similar force in the present day. The verse does not despise ancestors; it refuses to make age a substitute for understanding and guidance, preserving what is true while testing every inheritance by revelation. (31:14 — **“So be grateful to Me”**) In other words, the courage to break a harmful pattern answers inherited practice and revealed guidance.

---

## Verse 2:171

> The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding

**A PICTURE OF UNRECEIVED GUIDANCE**

For a picture of unreceived guidance, the decisive wording is ***“The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls”***. The verse gives a parable of people who hear the sound of revelation but do not grasp its meaning. A shepherd may call animals that hear a noise without understanding the words or the danger being addressed. In the same way, a person may listen to recitation, arguments, warnings, and reminders while allowing none of them to reach the heart. The comparison is not saying that all disbelievers lack physical hearing, speech, or sight. The Qur’an immediately uses *deaf, dumb, and blind* in a moral and spiritual sense. Their faculties function biologically, but they refuse to use them for guidance. The Qur’an elsewhere speaks of hearts that do not understand and ears that do not hear the truth despite being physically sound. A cry or shout can alert an animal without conveying a reasoned message. It may produce movement, fear, or temporary attention, but it does not produce insight. The parable describes people whose response to revelation is similarly shallow. They may react to a loud speaker, a social identity, or an emotional atmosphere without understanding what Allah is asking of them. This is a warning to Muslims as well. Recitation can become sound without reflection, sermons can become familiar background, and religious language can be repeated without repentance. The believer measures his choices by the Qur’an rather than taking repeated hearing as sufficient. (2:170 — **“if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance”**) Because a picture of unreceived guidance governs 2:171, the three blocked faculties arises from a picture of unreceived guidance. It follows that the messenger’s compassion completes a picture of unreceived guidance through the three blocked faculties.

**THE THREE BLOCKED FACULTIES**

Read under the three blocked faculties, the relevant clauses are ***“and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb”***. Hearing represents receiving evidence, speech represents acknowledging and responding to truth, and sight represents recognizing the signs that lead to Allah. When the three are described as blocked, the verse portrays a person who refuses to listen, will not confess what he knows, and does not see the meaning of the world around him. The blockage is not Allah’s injustice. It is connected to persistent rejection. When a person repeatedly turns away, his choices harden into a veil. The Qur’an says that when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. Divine judgement and human choice are both affirmed: people choose refusal, and Allah allows the consequences of their chosen path to settle upon them. The final phrase, *they do not understand*—*do not understand*, does not deny their ability to solve worldly problems. A person can be clever in business, science, or politics while failing to understand the purpose of life. Qur’anic understanding is *reason*: connecting signs to their Creator, controlling desire, and accepting moral consequence. Pride is one of the greatest barriers. The person who approaches revelation only to defeat it may notice details but miss its direction. The sincere person who seeks what his Lord wants can be guided even when he begins with limited knowledge. Understanding is therefore both an intellectual and moral act. (7:179 — **“Indeed, We have destined many jinn”**) The reason the messenger’s compassion follows the three blocked faculties lies in a picture of unreceived guidance. Therefore, the messenger’s compassion returns practical force to the three blocked faculties.

**THE MESSENGER’S COMPASSION**

The messenger’s compassion begins from ***“and blind so they have no understanding”***. The image also explains why prophets repeatedly called people despite rejection. They were not shouting meaningless sounds; they were conveying a clear message with patience. The Prophet ﷺ recited, explained, warned, encouraged, and answered questions. When people refused to hear, he grieved for them, but he did not force faith. Guidance belongs to Allah, while the messenger’s duty is clear conveyance. Muslim educators should follow this model. Teaching should be understandable, truthful, and connected to real life. A speaker should not rely only on volume, fear, or performance. The goal is for the listener to comprehend, reflect, and choose obedience. Spiritual deafness is not necessarily permanent while a person lives. The Qur’an invites people to listen attentively, reflect, and return. Turning off distractions, reading a translation with the Arabic, asking qualified questions, keeping good company, and practising what one learns can reopen the heart. The believer should make the supplication taught in the Qur’an: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes and make us an example for the mindful. A receptive heart is a gift, so one asks Allah for it while taking the means of receptivity. A radio may be switched on loudly in a room while its tuning remains between stations; sound fills the space, yet the message dissolves into noise. The call in this verse reaches ears in the same way when the faculties of response have been surrendered. Hearing syllables is not the same as receiving guidance. For a reader today, repeated exposure to sermons, recitation, and moral advice can create familiarity without obedience, so the test is not whether the sound was present but whether meaning crossed into judgement and action. (22:46 — **“Have they not travelled throughout the land”**) In other words, the messenger’s compassion answers a picture of unreceived guidance.

---

## Verse 2:172

> O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺

**LAWFUL PROVISION AS A SIGN OF WORSHIP**

The sequence reaches lawful provision as a sign of worship through ***“O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided”***. The preceding verse addressed all humanity; this one addresses believers specifically. Faith changes the way a person receives provision. Food is not merely fuel or pleasure. It is a gift from Allah, obtained through a chain of created means, and it should be consumed within the limits He has set. The command combines eating good things with gratitude, showing that bodily nourishment and spiritual worship are not enemies. Believers may enjoy lawful food without treating enjoyment as shameful. The Qur’an rejects ascetic inventions that declare Allah’s lawful adornments forbidden. At the same time, enjoyment must remain disciplined by moderation, health, justice, and gratitude. *Shukr* begins in the heart by recognizing Allah as the giver. It appears on the tongue through praise and the mention of His name, and it appears in action by consuming responsibly and using strength in obedience. Saying praise belongs to God after a meal is beautiful, but gratitude is incomplete if a person wastes food, hoards it while neighbours are hungry, or uses the resulting energy for oppression. The believer also thanks the people through whom provision arrives. Islam commands gratitude to parents, workers, hosts, farmers, and all who provide lawful benefit, while remembering that their ability is itself from Allah. Appreciation of created means does not compete with divine oneness; it is part of good character. (2:168 — **“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”**) Because lawful provision as a sign of worship governs 2:172, gratitude as proof of devotion arises from lawful provision as a sign of worship. It follows that food, justice, and community completes lawful provision as a sign of worship through gratitude as proof of devotion.

**GRATITUDE AS PROOF OF DEVOTION**

Gratitude as proof of devotion takes shape in ***“for you. And give thanks to Allah”***. The closing condition connects dietary practice to exclusive worship. If Allah alone is worshipped, then His servant accepts His guidance about what to consume rather than allowing appetite, fashion, or commercial pressure to define every limit. Worship is not confined to prayer in a mosque. Choosing lawful food, earning lawful income, and refusing exploitation can all become acts of worship when done for Allah. The phrase also prevents ritual from becoming disconnected from ethics. A person cannot claim that he worships Allah while deliberately consuming stolen wealth or supporting cruelty when lawful alternatives are available. What enters the body affects the heart, and the heart’s state affects worship. The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah is good and accepts only what is good, then described a traveller whose supplication is hindered by unlawful food, drink, clothing, and nourishment, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. The hadith places a high value on lawful provision. It does not mean that every poor person’s prayer is rejected or that every affluent person’s prayer is accepted. It warns that deliberate unlawful consumption can become a barrier to spiritual receptivity. The Prophet also taught moderation. The stomach should not be filled without restraint, and the believer should leave room for food, drink, and breath, according to the well-known report in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī. Moderation protects health and helps a person remain energetic for worship and service. (7:31 — **“Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat”**) The reason food, justice, and community follows gratitude as proof of devotion lies in lawful provision as a sign of worship. Therefore, food, justice, and community returns practical force to gratitude as proof of devotion.

**FOOD, JUSTICE, AND COMMUNITY**

The wording for food, justice, and community is ***“if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”***. Zakah, voluntary charity, fair wages, honest trade, and refusing food waste are expressions of gratitude. A society cannot praise *shukr* while allowing preventable hunger through greed or corruption. The Prophet ﷺ said that the one who is not concerned with the affairs of Muslims is not following the proper spirit of the community, and he encouraged feeding the hungry. The exact legal duties vary with circumstances, but the moral direction is clear: Allah’s gifts should circulate with mercy. The verse prepares for the specific prohibitions in the next āyah. Muslims do not invent dietary restrictions from superstition, caste, or religious competition. They follow what Allah has made lawful and unlawful, and they avoid both excess and negligence. A food is not spiritually powerful merely because a culture labels it so, nor is a lawful blessing made impure by baseless fear. A clean vessel can carry clean water, while a contaminated vessel spoils even what was pure when poured into it. Lawful food and thankful worship belong together in that way: what sustains the body enters the moral life rather than remaining a merely private purchase. Present-day supply chains can hide exploitation, fraud, or forbidden earnings behind attractive packaging, but concealment does not change the source. The verse asks the worshipper to care about the vessel of livelihood as seriously as the visible act of devotion. (16:114 — **“So eat from the good, lawful things”**) In other words, food, justice, and community answers lawful provision as a sign of worship.

---

## Verse 2:173

> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**CLEAR PROHIBITIONS**

***“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine”***, ***“and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah.”*** mark the turn toward clear prohibitions. This verse lists four primary categories of forbidden food: *maytah*, an animal that dies without lawful slaughter; flowing blood; swine; and an animal dedicated to other than Allah. The list establishes that dietary law is determined by revelation, not by superstition, ethnic pride, or personal taste. The phrase *He has only forbidden* also corrects people who invent unnecessary restrictions and then attribute them to Allah. The Qur’an gives related lists in 5:3, 6:145, and 16:115. The passages complement one another, while the Sunnah and juristic reasoning explain details such as lawful slaughter, hunting, impurities, and circumstances of necessity. A Muslim should learn from reliable scholarship rather than making confident rulings from a single translation. *Carrion* is an animal that dies without the prescribed process, though the jurists discuss exceptions such as certain sea animals and locusts based on authentic hadith. Flowing blood—flowing blood in 6:145—is prohibited, while blood that remains in the veins after proper slaughter is not treated in the same way. These distinctions show why Arabic wording, prophetic explanation, and legal method matter. The prohibition protects health, cultivates respect for life, and separates Muslim worship from pre-Islamic sacrificial customs. Slaughter is not a licence for cruelty. The Prophet ﷺ commanded excellence in slaughter, sharpening the blade, and sparing the animal unnecessary suffering, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. (2:172 — **“O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided”**) Because clear prohibitions governs 2:173, swine and sacrificial dedication arises from clear prohibitions. It follows that neither desiring nor transgressing completes clear prohibitions through swine and sacrificial dedication.

**SWINE AND SACRIFICIAL DEDICATION**

The verse develops swine and sacrificial dedication with ***“But if someone is compelled by necessity”***, ***“neither driven by desire”***. The flesh of swine is explicitly prohibited. Muslims accept the command as an act of obedience even where they do not know every wisdom. They may reflect upon hygiene, disease, and the moral symbolism of the prohibition, but they do not claim that an unproven explanation is the whole reason. Revelation is authoritative because Allah knows what His servants do not know. What has been dedicated to other than Allah concerns food offered as a sacrifice in the name of an idol, person, spirit, or other created object. The issue is theological as well as dietary. An act of sacrifice is worship, and worship belongs to Allah alone. Eating such a sacrifice would participate in or approve a rival allegiance, which contradicts *divine oneness*. Allah then gives an important concession: whoever is compelled by necessity may eat the forbidden food without sin, provided he neither desires it nor exceeds the need. *Necessity* occurs when a person faces a real danger to life or serious health and cannot find lawful food. Mere convenience, curiosity, social pressure, or a preference for forbidden taste is not necessity. The concession demonstrates that the divine law protects life. A person who would die or suffer severe harm without food may take enough to survive. He does not continue eating for pleasure once the danger is removed, and he does not turn the exception into a routine. The maxim *necessities permit the prohibited* is tied to genuine necessity and measured by its extent. (5:3 — **“what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall”**) The reason neither desiring nor transgressing follows swine and sacrificial dedication lies in clear prohibitions. Therefore, neither desiring nor transgressing returns practical force to swine and sacrificial dedication.

**NEITHER DESIRING NOR TRANSGRESSING**

At neither desiring nor transgressing, attention falls on ***“nor exceeding immediate need”***, ***“they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Neither desiring it nor exceeding the need is often explained as not seeking the forbidden item while lawful alternatives exist and not eating beyond what necessity requires. The person’s heart remains unwilling to violate the rule, and his action is restricted to preservation of life. If someone can obtain lawful food through asking, purchasing, travelling, or accepting help, he should do so. The concession also applies in a way that avoids harm to others. A person may not use emergency conditions as a licence to steal from someone more vulnerable, endanger another life, or profit from scarcity. Necessity removes the sin of the narrowly defined consumption; it does not suspend all other obligations. The verse ends with Allah’s forgiveness and mercy. The Lawgiver knows human weakness, accidents, travel, famine, coercion, and illness. Legal commands are not designed to trap a servant who is genuinely unable. The concession is not a loophole against obedience; it is part of obedience because Allah Himself revealed it. This principle extends across worship and social law. A sick person may pray sitting, a traveller may shorten prayer, and a person facing compulsion is judged according to what he could control. Mercy is embedded in the law while the normal rule remains clear. Necessity operates like an emergency exit: it is built to preserve life when the ordinary route is blocked, not to become the building's everyday entrance. The listed prohibitions remain real, yet the trapped person is not commanded to die in order to display obedience. That balance matters in present-day crises involving hunger, medicine, or isolation. Need must be genuine, the use no more than required, and the heart free of rebellion; within those limits, taking the exit is obedience to the merciful Lawgiver rather than escape from His law. (6:118 — **“So eat only of what is slaughtered in Allah’s Name”**) In other words, neither desiring nor transgressing answers clear prohibitions.

---

## Verse 2:174

> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment

**CONCEALMENT FOR WORLDLY GAIN**

Read under concealment for worldly gain, the relevant clauses are ***“Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them”***, ***“for a fleeting gain consume nothing”***. The passage returns to the betrayal of revealed knowledge. These people conceal what Allah sent down and exchange it for a small price. The *price* can be money, office, influence, political protection, social honour, or the preservation of an institution’s reputation. It is called small not because worldly wealth has no value at all, but because no temporary gain can compare with the truth and the eternal consequences of betraying it. The concealment is deliberate. The previous passages have distinguished sincere uncertainty from knowing refusal. Here, people possess revelation and hide it when making it known would cost them something. Religious authority becomes a marketplace, and the scripture is treated as an instrument for securing advantage rather than as a trust that judges the holder. Consume nothing but fire in their bellies is a severe image. The wealth acquired through the concealment may look like food, salary, or comfort in this life, but its unseen reality is fire because it was gained by selling guidance. The image also reverses the purpose of food in the preceding verses. Lawful provision nourishes a servant for worship; unlawful gain acquired through betrayal becomes a source of punishment. This does not mean that every teacher who receives a salary has sold religion. Scholars, educators, translators, and institutions may lawfully receive payment for their time and work. The warning concerns making revelation serve a dishonest bargain or suppressing truth specifically to obtain worldly advantage. The intention, knowledge, and conduct must be examined with justice. (2:159 — **“Those who hide the clear proofs”**) Because concealment for worldly gain governs 2:174, allah will not speak to them arises from concealment for worldly gain. It follows that the responsibility of religious speech completes concealment for worldly gain through allah will not speak to them.

**ALLAH WILL NOT SPEAK TO THEM**

Allah will not speak to them begins from ***“but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment”***, ***“nor will He purify them.”***. The statement that Allah will not speak to them is a declaration of humiliation and deprivation, not a denial that Allah knows or judges them. On the Day of Resurrection, the honour of divine address and acceptance is withheld from those who treated His words as commodities. The Qur’an elsewhere describes Allah speaking to believers with peace and honour, making the contrast profound. The verse should make people value truthful speech in the present. Those who manipulate scripture may receive applause from audiences, but they will not be able to purchase Allah’s approval. The servant should prefer an honest admission of limited knowledge to a confident answer designed to retain status. Purification—*tazkiyah*—can mean cleansing from sin and granting praise, acceptance, and growth. The concealment of guidance corrupts both the teacher and the community. The person may retain an outward religious identity, but the deliberate betrayal prevents him from receiving the purification that comes through sincere faith and repentance. Yet the next verse in this passage explains that repentance remains possible before death. The warning is not a barrier against return; it is a description of the unrepentant concealer. A person who recognizes his failure should expose the truth, repair the harm, and seek Allah’s forgiveness rather than defending the old falsehood. (3:187 — **“˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those”**) The reason the responsibility of religious speech follows allah will not speak to them lies in concealment for worldly gain. Therefore, the responsibility of religious speech returns practical force to allah will not speak to them.

**THE RESPONSIBILITY OF RELIGIOUS SPEECH**

***“And they will suffer a painful punishment”*** establish the responsibility of religious speech. This āyah applies to every field in which people claim Allah’s authority. A preacher may conceal a command because it would offend donors. A leader may hide a legal principle because it threatens his political alliance. A community may suppress abuse to protect its image. A writer may quote scripture selectively to sell a message. These are all forms of the danger described, though the precise judgement of each case belongs to Allah. The solution is *trust*: honest transmission, transparent sources, correction of mistakes, and willingness to say what is true even when it reduces worldly advantage. The Qur’an commands people to fulfil trusts and judge with justice. Religious knowledge is among the greatest trusts. The verse should not lead people to distrust every scholar or religious institution. Most knowledge is transmitted through human effort, and trustworthy teachers are necessary. Muslims should neither idolize teachers nor assume corruption without evidence. They evaluate claims, ask for proof, recognize expertise, and preserve good manners. A teacher’s livelihood can be lawful when it supports sincere service. The danger arises when money controls the conclusion or when the teacher knowingly hides a clear truth. The distinction protects both scholarship and the public from cynical suspicion. Concealed revelation is like a lighthouse keeper covering the lamp after receiving payment from ships that prefer darkness. The small wage may be collected on shore, but the keeper has traded away the very duty that gave him a place in the tower. Religious knowledge carries that public trust. Today, money, access, reputation, or institutional pressure can make selective silence appear prudent; the verse exposes the exchange as ruinous because what is consumed is not merely payment but fire joined to a hidden truth. (5:44 — **“Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance”**) In other words, the responsibility of religious speech answers concealment for worldly gain.

---

## Verse 2:175

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire

**A TERRIBLE EXCHANGE**

A terrible exchange takes shape in ***“They are the ones”***. A disastrous trade is being described: people who concealed revelation behave as merchants making a ruinous exchange. They give up guidance, and take *error*, misguidance. They abandon the possibility of Allah’s forgiveness and choose punishment. The language of trade continues from the *small price* in the preceding āyah: they believe they are gaining something, but the transaction is spiritual ruin. Guidance is not an abstract possession. It is the light by which a person knows his Lord, distinguishes right from wrong, and finds the path to forgiveness. Misguidance may offer immediate comfort, status, or profit, but it leaves the person unable to see the consequences of his choices. The exchange is therefore irrational when measured by the Hereafter, even if it looks profitable in the marketplace of this world. The contrast is exact. Allah’s forgiveness is available through faith, repentance, and righteous action. Punishment is the result of refusing that mercy and persisting in betrayal. A person who hides truth for a temporary advantage does not merely lose information; he turns away from the means by which he could be purified. The Qur’an never presents Allah’s forgiveness as scarce. It repeatedly calls people to repent and return. The tragedy described here is that the concealers knowingly exchange an open gift for a consequence they could have avoided. Their sin is not a lack of access to mercy but a preference for something lesser. (2:174 — **“Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them”**) Because a terrible exchange governs 2:175, the shock of their endurance arises from a terrible exchange. It follows that a warning to knowledge-bearers completes a terrible exchange through the shock of their endurance.

**THE SHOCK OF THEIR ENDURANCE**

The wording for the shock of their endurance is ***“who trade guidance for misguidance”***. The final expression—their astonishing endurance of the Fire—is an Arabic rhetorical exclamation. It does not praise them for admirable patience. It expresses astonishment and rebuke at their endurance and persistence upon a path that leads to the Fire. Some early exegetes explain it as amazement at their audacity in committing the acts that make punishment their outcome. The wording is powerful because people are often patient for worldly aims. They endure long hours for money, status, or entertainment, but may not endure the short discomfort of honesty, prayer, or repentance. The heart is made to compare the hardship accepted now with the consequence purchased for later. A person rarely announces, *I choose punishment.* He tells himself that the compromise is small, the audience will never know, or the truth can be addressed later. Satan makes the immediate price of integrity seem larger than the eternal price of betrayal. Repeated choices then make the false path feel normal. The remedy is honest accounting. Before accepting a benefit, the believer asks what he is being asked to conceal. Before repeating a religious claim, he asks whether it is supported. Before obeying an influential person, he asks whether the command agrees with Allah’s guidance. Regular repentance interrupts self-deception before it becomes a settled identity. (3:177 — **“Those who trade belief”**) The reason a warning to knowledge-bearers follows the shock of their endurance lies in a terrible exchange. Therefore, a warning to knowledge-bearers returns practical force to the shock of their endurance.

**A WARNING TO KNOWLEDGE-BEARERS**

The movement toward a warning to knowledge-bearers rests on ***“and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire”***. The immediate audience includes people entrusted with scripture, but the warning reaches every Muslim who knows a truth and chooses to distort it. A student may hide a fact to win a debate; a businessperson may use religious language to justify fraud; a parent may teach children a convenient custom while ignoring a clear obligation. The danger is not limited to scholars. Conversely, knowledge should not be shared irresponsibly. The one who speaks without competence can mislead even while believing he is spreading guidance. The safest path is to learn, verify, state the evidence accurately, and refer complex matters to those qualified. The exclamation is addressed to the living. The person who has taken a wrong path can still exchange misguidance for guidance through sincere repentance. He may have to surrender money, status, or the approval of a group, but Allah’s forgiveness is worth more than every worldly price. The Qur’an describes repentance as a return to the best trade, not a humiliation. A community should make such return possible by welcoming truthful correction, protecting those who expose wrongdoing, and refusing to make a person’s past the sole definition of his future. Accountability and mercy are not opposites when both are directed toward truth and reform. Two patients can sit beside the same physician: one accepts the diagnosis and begins treatment, while the other bribes an assistant to hide the report and then boasts that no illness was found. Guidance and mercy are like the offered treatment; choosing error and punishment is the deliberate refusal that follows disclosure. The contrast remains immediate today whenever evidence threatens a profitable habit or cherished identity. The loss is not that truth was unavailable, but that something else was preferred after the truth arrived. (9:111 — **“Allah has indeed purchased from the believers their lives”**) In other words, a warning to knowledge-bearers answers a terrible exchange.

---

## Verse 2:176

> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition

**REVELATION IS TRUTH**

The verse develops revelation is truth with ***“That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth.”***. The verse gives the reason for the punishment described above: Allah sent down the Book in truth—*with truth*. The revelation is true in its source, content, purpose, and judgement. It comes from the One who knows the human condition and shows people the way to worship, justice, and salvation. Because the Book is true, concealing or distorting it is not a minor intellectual error; it is a betrayal of reality. The Qur’an is also described as confirming earlier revelation and serving as a criterion over it. This means Muslims honour the original messages given to the prophets while recognizing the Qur’an as the final preserved revelation. *In truth* therefore includes continuity with the prophetic call and correction of human additions and distortions. Those who differ over the Book can refer to the People of the Book who disputed about the Qur’an, concealed its signs, or altered the meaning of their scripture. It can also include anyone who divides over revelation through denial, selective acceptance, invented interpretation, or conflict driven by worldly interest. Not every scholarly difference is condemned. The Qur’an itself recognizes sincere people who differ while seeking evidence, and the early jurists had legitimate disagreements in matters open to interpretation. The blameworthy *disagreement* is rooted in *deep opposition*, extreme opposition and hostility. It is not simply that two people reach different conclusions; it is that one side turns away from truth, breaks away from guidance, or uses disagreement to protect pride and power. A person can be wrong without being malicious, and he can be technically learned while being spiritually rebellious. (2:174 — **“Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them”**) Because revelation is truth governs 2:176, the book as a criterion arises from revelation is truth. It follows that unity around revelation completes revelation is truth through the book as a criterion.

**THE BOOK AS A CRITERION**

At the book as a criterion, attention falls on ***“And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition”***. The Qur’an does not merely settle arguments after they become public. It provides a criterion before the argument begins. Muslims return to it and the Sunnah to distinguish principle from custom, revelation from speculation, and genuine disagreement from factional rivalry. The Book also corrects the tendency to select isolated passages while ignoring the whole message of justice, mercy, worship, and accountability. A sound interpretation respects the Arabic text, the context of revelation, the Prophet’s explanation, the understanding of the Companions, and the principles of the religion. It avoids forcing the Qur’an to say what a political movement, personal desire, or inherited prejudice already decided. The one who approaches the Book with humility is more likely to benefit from its clarity. The fact that Allah sent the Book in truth does not mean that every person will accept it. Allah allows people a genuine moral response, and the Qur’an records those who believe, those who deny, and those who conceal what they know. Revelation is a proof and guidance; it does not remove the responsibility of choosing. Muslims invite without coercion, explain without distortion, and leave hearts to Allah. They should not manipulate evidence to force agreement, because the truth does not need dishonesty to support it. (3:103 — **“so that you may be ˹rightly˺ guided”**) The reason unity around revelation follows the book as a criterion lies in revelation is truth. Therefore, unity around revelation returns practical force to the book as a criterion.

**UNITY AROUND REVELATION**

The community’s unity is not achieved by suppressing every difference or demanding loyalty to a personality. It is achieved by returning together to Allah’s Book and the authentic Sunnah, maintaining justice and good manners when interpretation differs. The Qur’an commands holding fast collectively to Allah’s rope and not dividing into hostile factions. Where a matter is clear, believers should not manufacture controversy. Where a matter is genuinely interpretive, they should preserve brotherhood and avoid accusing one another of disbelief or corruption without valid grounds. The extreme opposition condemned in the verse is not the careful work of scholarship; it is the will to fight the Book rather than be corrected by it. Modern disputes can repeat the old pattern. A person may reject revelation because it challenges a social ideology, or quote it selectively to sanctify a political interest. Another may abandon the Qur’an’s ethical balance by turning one passage into a weapon against the rest. The remedy is to read the Book as a coherent revelation and to ask what Allah is requiring of the heart and society. The final authority belongs to Allah, not to the loudest faction. Every interpreter remains a servant who can be corrected. This humility is the opposite of *deep opposition*. A map torn into favoured pieces cannot guide a traveller across the whole country. Each fragment may contain real roads, yet the journey fails when disliked sections are discarded and isolated marks are made to contradict the map's design. The revealed Book is approached as a whole in the same way. In present-day argument, selective quotation can make almost any desire sound sacred; the verse locates the deepest division not in honest inquiry but in resistance that pulls a coherent gift into hostile fragments. (4:59 — **“then refer it to Allah”**) In other words, unity around revelation answers revelation is truth.

---

## Verse 2:177

> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE MEANING OF BIRR**

The meaning of birr begins from ***“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east”***, ***“or the west. Rather, the righteous are those”***, ***“who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books”***, ***“and the prophets”***. This āyah gives one of the Qur’an’s most comprehensive definitions of *birr*, righteousness and expansive goodness. It comes in the middle of the qiblah discussion, where people had argued about direction. Allah does not dismiss the qiblah; facing the commanded direction is part of obedience. He corrects the reduction of religion to an outward symbol while faith, charity, justice, and endurance are neglected. The verse begins with negation—righteousness is not *that you turn your faces*—then gives the complete positive definition. *Birr* includes sound belief, worship, social generosity, moral reliability, and steadfastness under pressure. A Muslim cannot choose one dimension and abandon the others. Ritual without mercy is hollow, and good intentions without worship are incomplete. The righteous person believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets. These are foundations of *īmān*. Belief in Allah gives life its purpose; belief in the Last Day gives actions consequence; belief in angels affirms an unseen order and accountability; belief in the revealed Books establishes guidance; and belief in all the prophets protects the unity of the prophetic mission. The list joins the final revelation to the whole history of revelation. Muslims do not believe in Muhammad ﷺ while rejecting Mūsā, ʿĪsā, Ibrāhīm, or the other messengers. They affirm the original messages given to them and accept the Qur’an as the final criterion. This faith is not a vague spirituality. It shapes how a person sees time, responsibility, suffering, and the rights of others. (2:215 — **“for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor”**) Because the meaning of birr governs 2:177, giving wealth despite love of it arises from the meaning of birr. It follows that fulfilling promises completes the meaning of birr through giving wealth despite love of it.

**GIVING WEALTH DESPITE LOVE OF IT**

***“who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars”***, ***“and for freeing captives”***, ***“who establish prayer, pay alms-tax”*** establish giving wealth despite love of it. The righteous give wealth—giving cherished wealth—despite loving it. The phrase recognizes that wealth is naturally attractive. Islam does not demand that people pretend money has no utility or that they have no affection for what they earned. It asks them to overcome possessiveness when another person has a legitimate need. The recipients are listed broadly. Relatives have a claim because generosity should begin with family without becoming tribal favoritism. Orphans need protection because they have lost parental care. The needy may lack sufficient provision. The traveller may be stranded far from resources. Those who ask should be treated with dignity, even when a person cannot give. Freeing captives points to liberation from unjust bondage and the restoration of human dignity. This spending includes obligatory alms and voluntary charity, though the verse’s wording is broader than alms alone. It can include food, medical assistance, debt relief, education, shelter, and advocacy for the oppressed. The aim is not only to transfer money but to remove vulnerability and restore people’s ability to live with dignity. The verse joins *prayer* and *alms*, as the Qur’an often does. Prayer repairs the servant’s relationship with Allah, while alms purifies wealth and repairs social relations. Giving alms means calculating it accurately, paying it to eligible recipients, and refusing to treat wealth as absolute ownership. The pairing prevents two distortions. A person cannot claim spirituality while neglecting the poor, and he cannot claim social activism while refusing the worship that gives justice its ultimate foundation. The body turns toward the qiblah, and wealth turns toward those whom Allah has made deserving. (59:7 — **“As for gains granted by Allah to His Messenger from the people of ˹other˺ lands, they are”**) The reason fulfilling promises follows giving wealth despite love of it lies in the meaning of birr. Therefore, fulfilling promises returns practical force to giving wealth despite love of it.

**FULFILLING PROMISES**

For fulfilling promises, the decisive wording is ***“and keep the pledges they make”***, ***“and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity”***, ***“and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they”***. *Those who fulfil their promises*—those who keep their pledges—are righteous. Trustworthiness includes personal promises, contracts, debts, covenants, employment agreements, marriage responsibilities, and public commitments. A believer does not use religious language to escape a written obligation or exploit a technical loophole against the purpose of an agreement. The Qur’an commands fulfilment of covenants and describes breaking promises as a sign of hypocrisy. The Prophet ﷺ identified breaking a promise as one of the signs of a hypocrite, while the hadith does not mean that every broken promise under every circumstance makes a person a hypocrite. It warns against making commitments carelessly or breaking them deliberately. The verse ends by naming patience in poverty, hardship, and battle. Poverty tests basic provision; hardship includes illness, fear, grief, and oppressive circumstances; battle tests courage, discipline, and moral restraint. The list shows that righteousness is proven when values are costly. Patience—*ṣabr*—does not mean accepting preventable oppression without action. The poor should be supported, the sick treated, and the oppressed defended. The patient person seeks lawful relief without abandoning faith, justice, or self-control. In war, patience includes refusing aggression, protecting non-combatants, honouring agreements, and stopping when justice requires it. Courage without restraint is not Qur’anic righteousness. (4:136 — **“Indeed, whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers”**)

**TRUTHFULNESS AND TAQWĀ**

Read under truthfulness and taqwā, the relevant clauses are ***“who are true ˹in faith˺”***, ***“and it is they”***, ***“who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. It describes a direction of life in which belief, worship, generosity, reliability, and patience support one another. A believer can fail and repent; he cannot make hypocrisy his settled method while claiming that external symbols alone prove righteousness. *They are the mindful*—*al-muttaqūn*. Mindfulness is awareness and protective obedience to Allah. It guards the believer from showing off in charity, abandoning prayer in private, breaking promises when no one can enforce them, or using hardship as an excuse for injustice. The final measure is not public appearance but sincerity before Allah. The verse is a charter of integrated faith. It includes creed without abstraction, ritual without formalism, charity without vanity, social duty without secular emptiness, and patience without passivity. The qiblah matters because Allah commands it, but it becomes spiritually meaningful when the person who faces it also faces poverty, injustice, temptation, and responsibility with truth. The Prophet ﷺ embodied this integration. He worshipped at night, fulfilled covenants, fed the poor, protected orphans, forgave when justice allowed, and stood firm under persecution. His Sunnah shows how the list becomes a life rather than a slogan. Righteousness is like a tree more than a painted sign. Faith is its root, worship gives it a trunk, generosity and fidelity spread as branches, and patience is the strength that keeps it standing in bad weather. A sign can point east or west while remaining lifeless; a tree proves itself by fruit and endurance. The verse gives present-day believers the same test: public symbols matter within obedience, but a religious appearance that never feeds the needy, keeps a promise, or withstands hardship has not reached the life described here. (2:285 — **“The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord”**) In other words, truthfulness and taqwā answers the meaning of birr.

---

## Verse 2:178
